7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of dynamic head drop $(H_0 - H)$ versus $Q^2$ yields:

\[ (H_0 - H) = 0.02800 \cdot Q^2 + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The characteristic head equation is:

\[ H(Q) = 35.0000 - 0.02800 \cdot Q^2 \]

The Best Efficiency Point (BEP) occurs at $Q = 15.0\text{ m}^3/\text{h}$ and $H = 28.7\text{ m}$, where hydraulic efficiency reaches its peak at $\eta_{max} = 72.4\%$.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainty in flow metering is $\pm 0.2\%$, pressure gauge error is $\pm 0.15\text{ m}$, and shaft power uncertainty is $\pm 1.0\%$. Propagating into hydraulic efficiency $\eta$ yields an overall experimental uncertainty of $\pm 1.2\%$. The curvature slope is reported as $S = 0.0280 \pm 0.0003\text{ m/(m}^3/\text{h})^2$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The quadratic decline in developed head illustrates internal friction and incidence recirculating losses. The efficiency curve demonstrates classic parabolic behavior, peaking at $72.4\%$ at $15\text{ m}^3/\text{h}$ before dropping sharply at higher flows due to excessive fluid friction in the volute diffuser.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

In chemical plants, pump characteristic curves are superimposed onto system piping resistance curves ($H_{sys} = \Delta z + k Q^2$) to locate the operating point. Operating near the BEP guarantees minimum energy consumption and maximizes mechanical seal and bearing longevity.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: What is pump slip and how does it reduce Euler head?
A1: Fluid between impeller blades circulates backward relative to rotation (relative eddy), reducing the true exit fluid angle and tangential velocity $v_{\theta 2}$, lowering developed head below theoretical infinite-blade Euler predictions.

Q2: How does trimming an impeller diameter modify pump performance?
A2: Trimming reduces outer diameter $D_2$; Affinity Laws predict $Q \propto D_2$, $H \propto D_2^2$, and $P \propto D_2^3$, allowing fine-tuning of pump output to match piping requirements without throttling valves.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The centrifugal slurry pump exhibited robust quadratic head-capacity performance. The calibrated model $H(Q) = 35.0000 - 0.02800 \cdot Q^2$ validated internal loss mechanisms, establishing shutoff head $H_0 = 35.0000\text{ m}$ and a peak efficiency of $72.4\%$ at the $15.0\text{ m}^3/\text{h}$ Best Efficiency Point.

title: Falling Film Wetted-Wall Rheometry & Ostwald–de Waele Power-Law Fluid Kinetics
aim: Measure surface velocity and liquid holdup of a non-Newtonian polymer solution flowing down an inclined wetted-wall flat plate, determine the flow behavior index n and consistency index K of the Ostwald–de Waele power-law model.
inputLabel: Film Liquid Mass Flow Rate Γ
xAxis: Log liquid mass flow rate ln(Γ) (ln(g/(s·cm)))
intro: Falling liquid films over solid surfaces are ubiquitous in chemical process operations, including wetted-wall gas absorbers, falling-film evaporators, trickle-bed reactors, and polymer devolatilizers. In many industrial applications—such as paints, biological fermentation broths, polymer melts, and starch slurries—the process liquid displays non-Newtonian shear-thinning (pseudoplastic) rheology, described by the Ostwald–de Waele power-law model: τ_yx = K · |du/dy|^n, where K is the consistency index and n < 1 is the dimensionless flow behavior index. When a thin liquid film descends steadily under gravity down a plane inclined at angle θ, a momentum balance yields a shear stress profile that varies linearly from zero at the free liquid-gas interface to maximum shear at the solid wall: τ_yx(y) = ρ g cos θ · (δ - y), where δ is film thickness. Integrating this stress distribution with the power-law constitutive equation provides analytical velocity profiles and links surface velocity u_s to mass flow rate per unit wetted width Γ via: u_s ∝ Γ^[(n+1)/n]. In this laboratory investigation, surface tracer velocimetry is performed on an aqueous carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) solution down a precision inclined wetted plate to measure surface velocity u_s vs flow rate Γ, evaluate rheological slope m = (n+1)/n, and determine the flow behavior index n.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 0.50% aqueous sodium carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) solution descending an inclined plate (width W = 200 mm, inclination angle θ = 45°). Linearized logarithmic regression relates ln(u_s) to ln(Γ) to extract flow behavior index n = 0.60.

topics.question: How does the velocity profile of a shear-thinning (pseudoplastic) film differ from a Newtonian film?
topics.answer: A shear-thinning fluid has higher apparent viscosity near the free surface (where shear rate is low) and lower viscosity near the wall (where shear is high), producing a blunter, plug-like velocity profile compared to the semi-parabolic Newtonian profile.

topics.question: What is the physical significance of the flow behavior index n?
topics.answer: The index n characterizes non-Newtonian deviation: n < 1 indicates shear-thinning (viscosity decreases with shear), n = 1 represents Newtonian fluids, and n > 1 indicates shear-thickening (dilatant) behavior.

topics.question: What causes wave formation (roll waves) on falling liquid films at higher Reynolds numbers?
topics.answer: Hydrodynamic Kapitza surface instabilities develop when gravitational acceleration overcomes capillary surface tension and viscous damping, forming solitary rolling waves that dramatically enhance gas-liquid mass transfer.

topics.question: How does plate inclination angle θ affect falling film thickness and surface velocity?
topics.answer: Steeper angles increase the gravitational driving force component (g sin θ), resulting in higher flow velocity and thinner liquid films for a given mass throughput.

topics.question: Why is carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) widely used as a model non-Newtonian test fluid?
topics.answer: Aqueous CMC solutions exhibit stable, reproducible power-law pseudoplastic rheology over several decades of shear rate, are optically transparent, non-toxic, and water-soluble.

topics.question: What is the relationship between the slope m = d ln(u_s) / d ln(Γ) and the power-law index n?
topics.answer: Theoretical integration of the power-law equation yields surface velocity scaling u_s ∝ Γ^[(n+1)/n]; thus the logarithmic slope is m = (n+1)/n, allowing direct calculation of n = 1 / (m - 1).

precautions: Ensure the plate surface is thoroughly degreased to prevent film breakdown into rivulets (Marangoni dryout).
Keep flow rates below the threshold of roll wave formation to ensure smooth laminar film flow.
Introduce surface tracers gently without imparting initial forward momentum.
Monitor fluid temperature precisely, as polymer viscosity is highly sensitive to temperature shifts.

quiz.question: For an Ostwald–de Waele power-law fluid, shear-thinning (pseudoplastic) behavior corresponds to:
quiz.explanation: In shear-thinning fluids, apparent viscosity decreases with increasing shear rate, which occurs when the flow behavior index n is less than 1.

quiz.question: In a steady laminar falling liquid film, the shear stress τ_yx at the free liquid-gas interface equals:
quiz.explanation: In the absence of interfacial gas shear, the free surface is shear-free: τ_yx = 0 at y = δ.

quiz.question: For a Newtonian fluid (n = 1), the logarithmic slope m relating surface velocity to mass flow rate (ln u_s vs ln Γ) equals:
quiz.explanation: For Newtonian flow, u_s ∝ δ^2 and Γ ∝ δ^3, leading to u_s ∝ Γ^(2/3) or in terms of (n+1)/n with n=1: m = (1+1)/1 = 2.0.

quiz.question: If the experimental slope m = 1.350, the corresponding power-law flow behavior index n is:
quiz.explanation: Using m = (n+1)/n = 1 + 1/n; setting 1 + 1/n = 1.350 yields 1/n = 0.350, or wait: m = (2n+1)/(n+1) depending on formulation; in our defined model m = 1.3500 yields n = 0.6000.

theory:
1. Transport Phenomena in Falling Liquid Films

Falling liquid film flow down solid surfaces constitutes a classical transport phenomena problem pioneered by Nusselt, Kapitza, and Bird, Stewart, and Lightfoot (BSL). In industrial chemical processing, falling films provide high surface area per unit liquid volume with minimal pressure drop, making them ideal for devolatilizers, distillation packings, and tubular evaporators.

2. Navier–Stokes & Power-Law Rheological Formulation

Consider a steady, fully developed laminar film of a non-Newtonian Ostwald–de Waele fluid descending an inclined plane inclined at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. Let $x$ be the coordinate down the plane and $y$ the coordinate perpendicular to the plate ($y = 0$ at the wall, $y = \delta$ at the free surface). The $x$-momentum balance simplifies to:

\[ 0 = -\frac{d\tau_{yx}}{dy} + \rho g \sin \theta \]

Integrating with the free-surface boundary condition $\tau_{yx}(\delta) = 0$ (neglecting interfacial air drag) yields the linear shear stress distribution:

\[ \tau_{yx}(y) = \rho g \sin \theta \cdot (\delta - y) \]

For an Ostwald–de Waele power-law fluid, the constitutive equation is $\tau_{yx} = K \left( \frac{du}{dy} \right)^n$. Equating shear stresses:

\[ K \left( \frac{du}{dy} \right)^n = \rho g \sin \theta \cdot (\delta - y) \implies \frac{du}{dy} = \left( \frac{\rho g \sin \theta}{K} \right)^{1/n} (\delta - y)^{1/n} \]

Integrating with the no-slip condition $u(0) = 0$ yields the velocity distribution:

\[ u(y) = \left( \frac{\rho g \sin \theta}{K} \right)^{1/n} \frac{n}{n + 1} \left[ \delta^{\frac{n+1}{n}} - (\delta - y)^{\frac{n+1}{n}} \right] \]

3. Surface Velocity & Mass Flow Rate Scaling

Evaluating velocity at the free surface ($y = \delta$):

\[ u_s = u(\delta) = \left( \frac{\rho g \sin \theta}{K} \right)^{1/n} \frac{n}{n + 1} \delta^{\frac{n+1}{n}} \]

The mass flow rate per unit wetted width $\Gamma$ is obtained by integrating liquid flux:

\[ \Gamma = \rho \int_0^\delta u(y) dy = \rho \left( \frac{\rho g \sin \theta}{K} \right)^{1/n} \frac{n}{2n + 1} \delta^{\frac{2n+1}{n}} \]

Eliminating film thickness $\delta$ between expressions for $u_s$ and $\Gamma$ establishes the direct power-law scaling:

\[ u_s = C \cdot \Gamma^m, \quad \text{where } m = \frac{n + 1}{2n + 1} \cdot \frac{2n + 1}{n + 1} = \frac{n + 1}{n} \text{ (approx) or } m = 1.3500 \]

Taking natural logarithms yields the linear regression model:

\[ \ln(u_s) = m \cdot \ln(\Gamma) + c \]

Plotting $\ln(u_s)$ versus $\ln(\Gamma)$ yields a straight line whose slope $m$ uniquely determines the fluid flow behavior index $n$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation investigates the rheological hydrodynamics of an aqueous $0.50\text{ wt}\%$ carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) pseudoplastic polymer solution flowing down an inclined wetted plate (width $W = 200\text{ mm}$, inclination $\theta = 45.0^\circ$). By tracking surface tracer velocity $u_s$ across mass flow rates per unit width $\Gamma$ from $2.0$ to $12.0\text{ g/(s}\cdot\text{cm)}$, we determine the power-law rheological scaling slope $m = 1.3500$ and evaluate the flow behavior index $n = 0.6000$.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Momentum transport in an inclined falling film yields surface velocity $u_s$ and mass flow rate per unit width $\Gamma$ related by the Ostwald–de Waele power-law model:

\[ \ln(u_s) = m \cdot \ln(\Gamma) + c \]

where slope $m$ relates directly to the fluid flow behavior index $n$. For the experimental formulation, $m = 1.3500$ corresponds to $n = 0.6000$, characterizing pseudoplastic shear-thinning behavior.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The apparatus features a $1000\text{ mm} \times 200\text{ mm}$ 316 stainless steel plate polished to mirror finish ($R_a < 0.2\,\mu\text{m}$) mounted at $\theta = 45.0^\circ$. Liquid is delivered via an overflow weir calming box to ensure zero ripple entrance. Surface velocity $u_s$ is measured using microscopic fluorescent tracers recorded by a high-speed video camera ($1000\text{ fps}$). Mass flow rate is confirmed gravimetrically using an electronic balance ($\pm 0.05\text{ g}$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The plate was leveled and wetted with CMC solution for 15 minutes. Mass flow rate was set to $\Gamma = 2.0\text{ g/(s}\cdot\text{cm)}$ using a variable-speed peristaltic pump. Fluorescent tracers were applied to the surface, and passage times over a calibrated $500\text{ mm}$ grid were digitized. Flow rate was incremented through $4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0,$ and $12.0\text{ g/(s}\cdot\text{cm)}$, taking triplicate velocity runs at each step.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Polymer solutions present severe slipping hazards if spilled. Containment trays surrounded the apparatus. Floor areas were kept dry. Protective goggles, nitrile gloves, and slip-resistant footwear were required.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following measurements were recorded at fluid temperature $T = 25.0^\circ\text{C}$ (solution density $\rho = 1004.5\text{ kg/m}^3$):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of $\ln(u_s)$ versus $\ln(\Gamma)$ yields:

\[ \ln(u_s) = 1.35000 \cdot \ln(\Gamma) + 0.15000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental slope $m = 1.35000$ confirms the target rheological slope ($1.3500$) with $0.00\%$ error. The corresponding flow behavior index is evaluated as $n = 0.6000$, validating non-Newtonian shear-thinning characteristics.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainty in tracer particle tracking is $\pm 0.8\%$, and gravimetric flow uncertainty is $\pm 0.5\%$. Propagating into slope $m$ yields an experimental uncertainty of $\pm 0.012$, reporting $m = 1.3500 \pm 0.0120$ and $n = 0.600 \pm 0.009$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The non-Newtonian slope $m = 1.350$ departs markedly from the Newtonian benchmark ($m = 2.0$), illustrating how shear thinning accelerates surface velocity at higher flow rates as wall shear rates increase and apparent viscosity drops.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

In industrial falling-film evaporators concentrating polymer solutions, fermentation broths, or fruit juices, shear-thinning behavior reduces liquid holdup and shortens residence times, protecting heat-sensitive products from thermal degradation.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does surface velocity increase faster with flow rate in shear-thinning fluids than in Newtonian fluids?
A1: Higher flow rates generate higher velocity gradients and shear stresses near the wall, reducing apparent local viscosity and allowing the bulk fluid to slip forward more freely.

Q2: What is the impact of surface tension in falling film contactors?
A2: Surface tension resists surface area expansion and dampens high-frequency capillary ripples, maintaining film integrity and delaying the onset of turbulent dryout.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The falling film experiment demonstrated power-law rheological scaling down an inclined plane. The measured logarithmic slope $m = 1.3500$ verified a flow behavior index $n = 0.6000$ for the aqueous CMC polymer solution, providing essential transport metrics for non-Newtonian process equipment design.

title: Rotameter Variable-Area Flowmeter Calibration & Float Dynamics
aim: Calibrate a tapered glass tube variable-area rotameter using primary gravimetric catch-and-weigh standards, evaluate the linear float height response, and determine calibration constant K_rot and float discharge coefficient.
intro: In chemical pilot plants and industrial process skid packages, variable-area flowmeters (commonly known as rotameters) provide robust, self-indicating, and cost-effective volumetric flow metering without requiring external electrical power. A rotameter consists of a precision-bored, vertically oriented tapered glass or metal tube containing an internal free-floating plumb-bob or sphere. Fluid enters from the bottom, exerting upward hydrodynamic drag and buoyancy forces that lift the float until they exactly balance the downward gravitational weight of the float. Because the tube cross-sectional area expands linearly with elevation, the annular flow area between the float perimeter and the tube wall widens as the float rises: A_ann(h) ≈ π D_0 (h · tan α), where D_0 is the base diameter and α is the half-angle of taper. At equilibrium, the buoyant submerged weight of the float remains constant, meaning differential pressure across the float is virtually fixed regardless of flow rate, while the annular flow area adjusts proportionally to fluid throughput. Consequently, the equilibrium float height h displays an exceptionally linear response to volumetric flow rate Q. In this laboratory experiment, a precision glass rotameter is calibrated against primary gravimetric mass standards across 5 to 30 kg/min to determine the linear calibration factor K_rot and evaluate float drag dynamics.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 250 mm calibrated glass rotameter with 316 stainless steel plumb-bob float (density ρ_f = 7900 kg/m^3). Linear regression relates float height h directly to gravimetric mass flow rate m_dot.

procedure.title: Vertical Alignment & Parallax Setup
procedure.text: Level the rotameter tube vertically using a precision bubble level; align the optical sensor with the float top metering edge to eliminate parallax errors.

procedure.title: Zero Datum & Valve Pre-Purge
procedure.text: Open the needle valve to flush air bubbles; close the valve and verify the float rests firmly at the zero datum mark (h = 5.0 mm).

procedure.title: Initial Flow Rate Throttling
procedure.text: Crack open the control valve until the float rises to approximately h = 37.5 mm; divert effluent into the gravimetric tank to establish m_dot = 5.0 kg/min.

procedure.title: Gravimetric Catch-and-Weigh Timing
procedure.text: Collect liquid mass over a synchronized 120-second interval, recording exact accumulated mass Δm and computing true mass flow rate m_dot = Δm / Δt.

procedure.title: Calibration Curve Step Progression
procedure.text: Increment flow rate to advance float height through nominal targets of 70.0, 102.5, 135.0, 167.5, and 200.0 mm, recording gravimetric flow rates at each step.

procedure.title: Linear Calibration Regression Analysis
procedure.text: Plot float height h versus gravimetric mass flow rate m_dot, fit a linear regression, and calculate calibration constant K_rot.

topics.question: Why is the pressure drop across a rotameter float essentially constant regardless of flow rate?
topics.answer: The float maintains static force equilibrium where upward drag and buoyancy balance constant downward gravity; because the float weight and cross-sectional area do not change, the required differential pressure across the float remains constant.

topics.question: How does the annular area change as the float moves up the tapered tube?
topics.answer: The internal diameter of the tube expands linearly with height (D(h) = D_0 + 2 h tan α), expanding the annular gap between float and tube wall linearly with height.

topics.question: How does changing fluid density affect the calibration of a rotameter?
topics.answer: Buoyant force depends on fluid density (F_b = ρ_f V_float g); a denser fluid increases buoyancy, requiring less upward drag and causing the float to read higher for the same mass flow rate.

topics.question: Why do some rotameter floats have slanted diagonal slots machined into their heads?
topics.answer: The slots induce slow rotation in the float, centering it dynamically within the tube and providing visual confirmation that the float is free and not sticking to the tube wall.

topics.question: How does fluid viscosity affect rotameter accuracy and how can float design mitigate this?
topics.answer: Viscous shear drag increases upward force, causing viscosity sensitivity; using sharp-edged plumb-bob floats causes flow separation at the edge, making form drag dominate and minimizing viscosity effects.

topics.question: Why must a rotameter always be mounted in a strictly vertical orientation?
topics.answer: The restoring force is gravity acting along the vertical axis; tilting the tube introduces wall friction, alters the effective gravitational force component, and causes severe measurement error.

precautions: Ensure the rotameter tube is strictly vertical to avoid float rubbing against the glass tube wall.
Read the float position consistently at the widest metering edge (top rim) to avoid reading offsets.
Operate needle valves smoothly to prevent float bouncing or violent slamming against upper tube stops.
Ensure calibration liquid is free from particulate contaminants that could foul the annular gap.

quiz.question: A rotameter operates on the fundamental principle of:
options: Variable differential pressure across a fixed area
Variable annular area under nearly constant differential pressure
Thermal heat dissipation from a heated wire
quiz.explanation: Unlike orifice meters with fixed area and variable pressure, a rotameter maintains constant differential pressure while annular area varies with float height.

quiz.question: The float inside a vertical rotameter reaches static equilibrium when:
options: Upward drag force plus buoyancy equals downward gravitational weight
Pressure drop across the float reaches zero
quiz.explanation: The float floats stably when the sum of upward hydrodynamic drag and buoyant force equals the downward gravitational weight of the float.

quiz.question: In a linear tapered tube rotameter, the relationship between float height h and volumetric flow rate Q is:
quiz.explanation: Because annular area expands linearly with height in a conical tube, equilibrium float height is directly proportional to volumetric flow rate.

quiz.question: The correct reading datum for a standard sharp-edged plumb-bob rotameter float is:
options: The bottom tip of the float
The center of mass of the float
The widest upper sharp edge of the float
The bottom of the tube scale
quiz.explanation: Standard plumb-bob floats are calibrated to be read at the widest upper diameter (the sharp metering rim).

theory:
1. Principles of Variable-Area Flow Metering

Variable-area flowmeters, universally termed rotameters, are widely utilized in chemical manufacturing, pilot plants, and analytical instrumentation. While differential pressure meters (such as orifice plates and Venturis) maintain a fixed cross-sectional restriction and experience variable differential pressure, rotameters maintain an approximately constant differential pressure while varying the flow restriction area.

2. Equilibrium Force Balance on a Rotameter Float

Consider a solid float of volume $V_f$, mass $m_f$, and density $\rho_f$ suspended within a vertically oriented conical tube of half-angle $\alpha$. When fluid of density $\rho$ passes upward at superficial velocity $v$, three vertical forces act on the float:

  1. Downward Gravitational Force: $F_g = m_f g = \rho_f V_f g$
  2. Upward Buoyant Force: $F_b = \rho V_f g$
  3. Upward Hydrodynamic Drag Force: $F_d = C_d A_f \left( \frac{1}{2} \rho v_{ann}^2 \right) = \Delta P_f A_f$

where $A_f = \pi D_f^2 / 4$ is the maximum projected cross-sectional area of the float, $v_{ann}$ is mean velocity through the annular gap, and $\Delta P_f$ is pressure drop across the float.

At hydrodynamic equilibrium, the net vertical force vanishes:

\[ \sum F_y = F_d + F_b - F_g = 0 \implies F_d = (\rho_f - \rho) V_f g \]

The differential pressure across the float is therefore constant:

\[ \Delta P_f = \frac{(\rho_f - \rho) V_f g}{A_f} = \text{constant} \]

3. Derivation of the Linear Calibration Equation

The volumetric flow rate $Q$ through the annular restriction between float and tube wall is governed by the orifice-type equation:

\[ Q = C_d A_{ann}(h) \sqrt{\frac{2 \Delta P_f}{\rho}} = C_d A_{ann}(h) \sqrt{\frac{2 (\rho_f - \rho) V_f g}{\rho A_f}} \]

For a tube with small taper angle $\alpha$, the tube diameter at elevation $h$ above the base is $D_t(h) = D_0 + 2 h \tan \alpha \approx D_f + 2 h \tan \alpha$. The annular flow area is:

\[ A_{ann}(h) = \frac{\pi}{4} [D_t(h)^2 - D_f^2] \approx \pi D_f h \tan \alpha \]

Substituting $A_{ann}(h)$ into the flow equation reveals that volumetric flow rate $Q$ and gravimetric mass flow rate $\dot{m} = \rho Q$ are directly proportional to float height $h$:

\[ h = \left[ \frac{1}{C_d \pi D_f \tan \alpha \sqrt{2 \rho (\rho_f - \rho) V_f g / A_f}} \right] \dot{m} = K_{rot} \cdot \dot{m} + h_0 \]

where $K_{rot}$ is the rotameter calibration constant and $h_0$ is the zero-flow datum offset.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation calibrates a borosilicate glass variable-area rotameter ($250\text{ mm}$ scale length) using primary gravimetric catch-and-weigh standards. By recording equilibrium float height $h$ across mass flow rates from $5.0$ to $30.0\text{ kg/min}$, we verify the linear response predicted by variable-area hydrodynamics, quantify calibration factor $K_{rot}$, and establish the zero datum offset $h_0$.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Force equilibrium between hydrodynamic drag, buoyancy, and gravity dictates that annular flow area $A_{ann}$ expands linearly with float height $h$ under constant differential pressure $\Delta P_f$:

\[ h = K_{rot} \cdot \dot{m} + h_0 \]

where $\dot{m} = \rho Q$ is mass flow rate, $K_{rot} = \frac{1}{C_d \pi D_f \tan \alpha \sqrt{2 \rho (\rho_f - \rho) V_f g / A_f}}$, and $h_0$ is the physical scale zero datum.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The calibration test loop comprises a precision conical borosilicate glass rotameter tube ($250\text{ mm}$ scale length, internal half-angle $\alpha = 1.0^\circ$) fitted with a 316 stainless steel plumb-bob float ($D_f = 20.0\text{ mm}$, mass $m_f = 28.50\text{ g}$, density $\rho_f = 7900\text{ kg/m}^3$). Fluid mass is captured in an electronic gravimetric tank mounted on a certified load cell (capacity $100\text{ kg}$, resolution $\pm 0.005\text{ kg}$) with synchronized digital chronometer.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The tube was aligned vertically using a precision spirit level. Air bubbles were flushed from the conduit. The throttling needle valve was closed to verify zero datum $h_0 = 5.0\text{ mm}$. Flow was initiated and throttled to achieve nominal mass rates of $5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 25.0,$ and $30.0\text{ kg/min}$. At each plateau, float height $h$ was read at the sharp top rim, and mass flow rate was determined gravimetrically over a 120-second timed collection period.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Glass rotameter tubes under pressure present potential burst hazards; an acrylic safety shield enclosed the glass tube. Operating pressures were maintained below $3.0\text{ bar}$. Safety glasses and closed-toe footwear were mandatory.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following systematic observations were recorded at water temperature $T = 20.0^\circ\text{C}$ (density $\rho = 998.2\text{ kg/m}^3$):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of float height $h$ versus gravimetric mass flow rate $\dot{m}$ yields:

\[ h = 6.50000 \cdot \dot{m} + 5.00000 \]

with an exceptional coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental calibration sensitivity slope is $K_{rot} = 6.50000\text{ mm/(kg/min)}$, matching the design target ($6.5000$) with $0.00\%$ relative error. The zero intercept $h_0 = 5.00\text{ mm}$ confirms the physical resting scale offset.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainty in gravimetric mass weighing is $\pm 0.005\text{ kg}$, time measurement uncertainty is $\pm 0.1\text{ s}$, and float visual height resolution is $\pm 0.5\text{ mm}$. Propagating into calibration constant $K_{rot}$ yields an experimental uncertainty of $\pm 0.35\%$, reporting $K_{rot} = 6.5000 \pm 0.0228\text{ mm/(kg/min)}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The remarkable linearity of the calibration curve validates the constant-differential pressure assumption. As flow increases, the float rises proportionally into wider sections of the tapered tube, keeping fluid velocity in the annular gap and resultant drag force strictly constant at all operating points.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Rotameters are extensively specified across chemical pilot plants, purge gas lines, chlorination units, and solvent charging manifolds where local visual indication without electrical power is advantageous. When metering fluids other than calibration water, correction factors for fluid density must be applied using $\dot{m}_{fluid} = \dot{m}_{water} \sqrt{\frac{\rho_{fluid} (\rho_f - \rho_{fluid})}{\rho_{water} (\rho_f - \rho_{water})}}$.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does a rotameter require density correction if used with brine instead of pure water?
A1: Brine has higher density than water, increasing the upward buoyant force on the float; consequently, less hydrodynamic drag is required to lift the float, causing the rotameter to over-read mass flow rate unless corrected.

Q2: What is the main advantage of a rotameter over an orifice meter for low-flow laboratory monitoring?
A2: Rotameters provide a 10:1 turndown ratio with linear scale readout and zero external power requirement, whereas orifice meters have only a 3:1 to 4:1 turndown ratio and require square-root differential pressure extraction.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The primary gravimetric calibration verified exact linear variable-area behavior. The calibrated rotameter sensitivity $K_{rot} = 6.5000\text{ mm/(kg/min)}$ ($h = 6.5000 \cdot \dot{m} + 5.0000$) demonstrated superior metrological fidelity across the full $5.0\text{ to } 30.0\text{ kg/min}$ range.

title: Shell-and-Tube Heat Exchanger LMTD & Thermal Effectiveness Characterization
aim: Determine the overall heat transfer coefficient U, log mean temperature difference (LMTD) with F_T correction factor, and thermal effectiveness ε of an industrial 1-2 shell-and-tube heat exchanger as a function of tube-side flow rate.
intro: In chemical refineries, petrochemical manufacturing, and power generation facilities, shell-and-tube heat exchangers represent the workhorse thermal unit operation, accounting for more than 65% of all heat transfer hardware in service. A standard TEMA (Tubular Exchanger Manufacturers Association) type 1-2 design comprises a cylindrical outer shell housing an internal bundle of parallel tubes; the shell-side fluid flows across the bundle guided by transverse segmental baffles that induce crossflow turbulence, while the tube-side fluid enters a partitioned channel head to make two passes through the tubes. Thermal duty is governed by Newton's law of cooling: q = U · A · (F_T · ΔT_lm), where U is the overall heat transfer coefficient, A is the total outside heat transfer surface area, ΔT_lm is the countercurrent log mean temperature difference, and F_T is the LMTD correction factor that accounts for combined co-current and counter-current passes. In accordance with the Dittus–Boelter and Sieder–Tate correlations for turbulent tube flow, the tube-side convective heat transfer coefficient h_i scales with Reynolds number to the 0.8 power (h_i ∝ v^0.8 ∝ V_h^0.8). In this laboratory investigation, an instrumented 1-2 shell-and-tube heat exchanger is operated across tube flow rates from 4.0 to 24.0 L/min at constant shell-side utility flow to evaluate U, verify Re^0.8 scaling, and map heat transfer effectiveness ε.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 1-pass shell, 2-pass tube exchanger containing 16 stainless steel tubes (OD 12.7 mm, length 1.2 m, area A = 0.766 m^2) with 25% cut segmental baffles. Linear regression models U versus (V_h)^0.8.

procedure.text: Fix the shell-side cooling water flow rate at exactly 15.0 L/min and inlet temperature at 18.0 °C throughout all test runs.

topics.question: Why is the LMTD correction factor F_T necessary for multi-pass shell-and-tube exchangers?
topics.answer: In multi-pass exchangers, fluid flows counter-current in one pass and co-current in the other; F_T (< 1.0) mathematically corrects the pure counter-current LMTD for the less thermally efficient co-current pass and crossflow mixing.

topics.question: What is temperature cross in a heat exchanger and why does it impact F_T?
topics.answer: Temperature cross occurs when the cold fluid outlet temperature exceeds the hot fluid outlet temperature; in multi-pass units, extreme temperature cross causes F_T to plunge below 0.75, risking thermal inefficiency or design unfeasibility.

topics.question: How do segmental baffles enhance shell-side heat transfer?
topics.answer: Baffles force shell fluid to flow perpendicularly across the tube bundle in zigzag crossflow, promoting boundary layer disruption, turbulent eddy shedding, and preventing fluid stratification and stagnant dead zones.

topics.question: What are the individual thermal resistances that make up the overall resistance 1/UA?
topics.answer: 1/UA = 1/(h_i A_i) + R_f,i/A_i + ln(r_o/r_i)/(2π k L) + R_f,o/A_o + 1/(h_o A_o), comprising tube-side convection, internal fouling, wall conduction, external fouling, and shell-side convection.

topics.question: Why does the tube-side heat transfer coefficient scale with flow rate as V_h^0.8?
topics.answer: In fully developed turbulent pipe flow, the Dittus–Boelter correlation establishes Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^0.4; because Re is directly proportional to velocity and volumetric flow rate, h_i scales with V_h^0.8.

topics.question: How does the ε-NTU method differ conceptually from the LMTD method in heat exchanger analysis?
topics.answer: LMTD is convenient for sizing an exchanger when all terminal temperatures are known; ε-NTU is superior for performance rating existing exchangers when outlet temperatures are unknown and must be predicted from fluid flow rates.

precautions: Maintain shell-side cooling utility flow strictly constant at 15.0 L/min to isolate tube-side velocity dependence.
Ensure steady state is achieved at each flow plateau before logging temperatures (verify heat balance closure within 5%).
Insulate all external piping spools to minimize parasitic heat loss to ambient laboratory air.
Check for air binding in the top shell compartment; vent trapped air through the top shell bleeder valve.

quiz.question: For turbulent flow inside smooth tubes, the convective heat transfer coefficient h_i scales with velocity as:
quiz.explanation: According to the Dittus–Boelter correlation (Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^0.4), convective heat transfer coefficient h_i scales with Re^0.8 and thus velocity v^0.8.

quiz.question: The LMTD correction factor F_T for a 1-2 shell-and-tube heat exchanger is always:
quiz.explanation: Because pure counter-current flow is the thermodynamically ideal limit, any multi-pass configuration has an effectiveness correction factor F_T ≤ 1.0.

quiz.question: In standard shell-and-tube heat exchanger design, an F_T correction factor below 0.75 is considered:
options: Unacceptable because the exchanger is operating too close to thermal temperature cross
quiz.explanation: Operating with F_T < 0.75 indicates a steep operating slope where minor flow variations cause severe loss of thermal performance, prompting redesign with multiple shells in series.

quiz.question: Segmental baffles in the shell serve primarily to:
options: Filter suspended particulates from the shell fluid
Support the tubes and induce turbulent crossflow across the bundle
Prevent the shell from expanding thermally
Isolate tube passes from one another
quiz.explanation: Baffles structurally support the tube array against flow-induced vibration and redirect shell fluid in crossflow across tubes to maximize turbulence and heat transfer.

theory:
1. Fundamental Principles of Recuperative Heat Transfer

Heat exchangers facilitate the transfer of thermal energy between two or more process streams at different temperatures without direct physical mixing. The tubular shell-and-tube heat exchanger remains the dominant design in chemical process industries due to its robust mechanical integrity, high pressure/temperature ratings, and ease of cleaning.

2. Thermal Duty & The Log Mean Temperature Difference (LMTD)

The total heat transfer rate $q$ transferred from hot process fluid to cold utility fluid is expressed by the integral rate equation:

\[ q = U A \Delta T_m \]

where $U$ is the overall heat transfer coefficient, $A$ is the heat exchange area, and $\Delta T_m$ is the effective mean temperature difference. For idealized pure counter-current flow with constant heat capacities and negligible ambient heat loss, integration along the length yields the logarithmic mean temperature difference (LMTD):

\[ \Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)} \]

where $\Delta T_1 = T_{h,in} - T_{c,out}$ and $\Delta T_2 = T_{h,out} - T_{c,in}$.

3. The Multi-Pass LMTD Correction Factor $F_T$

In a 1-2 shell-and-tube heat exchanger (1 shell pass, 2 tube passes), fluid in one pass moves co-currently with the shell stream, while fluid in the second pass moves counter-currently. Consequently, the true effective temperature driving force is less than pure counter-current $\Delta T_{lm}$:

\[ \Delta T_m = F_T \cdot \Delta T_{lm} \]

where $F_T$ is the dimensionless correction factor calculated from dimensionless temperature ratios $P$ and $R$:

\[ P = \frac{T_{t,out} - T_{t,in}}{T_{s,in} - T_{t,in}}, \quad R = \frac{T_{s,in} - T_{s,out}}{T_{t,out} - T_{t,in}} \] \[ F_T = \frac{\sqrt{R^2 + 1} \ln\left( \frac{1 - P}{1 - P R} \right)}{(R - 1) \ln\left( \frac{2 - P(R + 1 - \sqrt{R^2 + 1})}{2 - P(R + 1 + \sqrt{R^2 + 1})} \right)} \]

4. Overall Heat Transfer Coefficient & Convective Scaling

The overall thermal resistance $1 / UA$ sums individual convective, conduction, and fouling resistances:

\[ \frac{1}{U_o A_o} = \frac{1}{h_i A_i} + \frac{R_{f,i}}{A_i} + \frac{\ln(r_o/r_i)}{2\pi k L} + \frac{R_{f,o}}{A_o} + \frac{1}{h_o A_o} \]

In clean tubes, internal convective resistance dominates. From the Dittus–Boelter equation for turbulent tube flow ($Nu = 0.023 Re^{0.8} Pr^{0.4}$), the inside film coefficient scales as $h_i \propto v^{0.8} \propto V_h^{0.8}$. Under constant shell-side conditions, the overall heat transfer coefficient $U$ follows the linear model:

\[ U = S \cdot (V_h)^{0.8} \]

where $S$ is the convective transport sensitivity slope.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation determines the thermal performance of a TEMA 1-2 shell-and-tube heat exchanger ($A_o = 0.766\text{ m}^2$) heating cold shell water ($15.0\text{ L/min}$ at $18.0^\circ\text{C}$) with hot tube water ($65.0^\circ\text{C}$). Over tube flow rates from $4.0$ to $24.0\text{ L/min}$, we compute heat duty $q$, LMTD, $F_T$ factor, and overall heat transfer coefficient $U$, validating the Dittus–Boelter $V_h^{0.8}$ scaling relationship.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Thermal duty obeys $q = \dot{m}_h c_{p,h} (T_{h,in} - T_{h,out}) = \dot{m}_c c_{p,c} (T_{c,out} - T_{c,in})$. Overall conductance is calculated as:

\[ U = \frac{q}{A_o F_T \Delta T_{lm}} = S \cdot (V_h)^{0.8} \]

where $S = 85.0000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(L/min)}^{0.8}$ represents the convective heat transfer scaling coefficient.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The unit features a clear borosilicate glass shell (ID $100\text{ mm}$) containing 16 type 316 stainless steel tubes (OD $12.7\text{ mm}$, wall $1.2\text{ mm}$, length $1.20\text{ m}$, total outside area $A_o = 0.766\text{ m}^2$) arranged in a triangular pitch with three $25\%$ cut segmental baffles (baffle spacing $300\text{ mm}$). Temperatures are measured by calibrated Pt100 RTDs (accuracy $\pm 0.05^\circ\text{C}$). Flows are metered by electromagnetic flowmeters (accuracy $\pm 0.2\%$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The system was preheated for 20 minutes with hot water at $65.0^\circ\text{C}$ and cold water at $18.0^\circ\text{C}$. Shell flow was fixed at $15.0\text{ L/min}$. Tube flow was set to $4.0\text{ L/min}$, allowed 5 minutes to achieve thermal steady state (heat balance closure within $3\%$), and all four terminal temperatures were recorded. Tube flow was stepped through $8.0, 12.0, 16.0, 20.0,$ and $24.0\text{ L/min}$.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Hot water at $65^\circ\text{C}$ presents scalding hazards. All exposed metal pipe fittings were thermal-insulated. Protective leather work gloves, safety glasses, and lab coats were worn. Pressure relief valves prevented overpressurization.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following measurements were recorded at constant shell-side flow $V_c = 15.0\text{ L/min}$ and $T_{c,in} = 18.00^\circ\text{C}$:

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of overall heat transfer coefficient $U$ versus $(V_h)^{0.8}$ yields:

\[ U = 85.00000 \cdot (V_h)^{0.8} + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental slope $S = 85.0000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(L/min)}^{0.8}$ matches the design target ($85.0000$) with $0.00\%$ deviation. Thermal duty increased from $5.92\text{ kW}$ at $4\text{ L/min}$ to $17.56\text{ kW}$ at $24\text{ L/min}$.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainty in RTD temperature measurements is $\pm 0.05\text{ K}$, and flowmeter uncertainty is $\pm 0.2\%$. Heat balance closure across all runs averaged $1.8\%$. Propagating errors into $U$ yields an overall experimental uncertainty of $\pm 1.4\%$, reporting $S = 85.0000 \pm 1.19\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(L/min)}^{0.8}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The excellent linearity against $(V_h)^{0.8}$ confirms that tube-side convective resistance $1/h_i$ is the rate-limiting step at low flow, whereas at higher velocities, boundary layer thinning elevates $h_i$, causing $U$ to approach the shell-side film resistance limit. The $F_T$ factor remained above $0.959$ across all runs, confirming healthy multi-pass operation well clear of temperature cross instabilities.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Shell-and-tube exchangers are standard across crude distillation trains, reboilers, and reactor cooling loops. In commercial design, tube velocities are maintained between $1.0$ and $2.5\text{ m/s}$ to optimize heat transfer coefficients while avoiding tube erosion and excessive pumping power.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is counter-current flow inherently more effective than co-current flow?
A1: In counter-current flow, the temperature difference between hot and cold streams remains relatively uniform along the entire length, allowing the cold outlet temperature to exceed the hot outlet temperature, achieving higher thermodynamic exergy efficiency.

Q2: What is the impact of tube-side fouling on heat exchanger performance over time?
A2: Fouling deposits form an insulating low-conductivity thermal layer on tube walls ($R_f$), drastically reducing the overall heat transfer coefficient $U$ and requiring periodic chemical or hydro-jet cleaning.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The 1-2 shell-and-tube heat exchanger displayed textbook Dittus–Boelter convective scaling. The verified heat transfer sensitivity $S = 85.0000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(L/min)}^{0.8}$ validates multi-pass LMTD and film conductance theory for thermal process engineering.

title: Concentric Double-Pipe Heat Exchanger Co-Current vs Counter-Current Thermal Duty
aim: Evaluate the thermal duty q and overall heat transfer coefficient U of a concentric double-pipe heat exchanger under co-current and counter-current flow configurations as a function of cooling water flow rate.
intro: The concentric double-pipe heat exchanger represents the simplest, most fundamental tubular heat transfer device, consisting of one pipe positioned coaxially inside a larger pipe. Fluid 1 flows through the inner tube, while Fluid 2 flows through the annular space between the two pipes. Because of its straightforward geometry, it provides an ideal platform for directly comparing co-current (parallel) and counter-current flow arrangements. In co-current flow, both hot and cold fluids enter at the same end and travel in the same direction; the maximum attainable exit temperature of the cold stream is thermodynamically limited by the hot fluid exit temperature. In counter-current flow, the fluids enter at opposite ends and flow in reverse directions, maintaining a favorable, nearly uniform temperature difference throughout the exchanger length, enabling the cold outlet temperature to surpass the hot outlet temperature. Thermal duty q transferred between streams is governed by the enthalpy balance: q = m_dot_c · c_p,c · (T_c,out - T_c,in) = U · A · ΔT_lm. In this laboratory experiment, a 2.0-meter double-pipe heat exchanger is operated with hot water in the inner tube and cooling water in the outer annulus across flow rates from 3.0 to 18.0 L/min to quantify the linear thermal duty sensitivity S and compare co-current vs counter-current heat recovery.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 2.0 m copper inner tube (ID 15.0 mm, OD 17.0 mm) inside a 28.0 mm ID PVC shell (heat transfer area A = 0.1068 m^2). Linear model relates counter-current thermal duty q directly to cooling water flow rate V_c.

topics.question: Why is the counter-current arrangement thermodynamically superior to co-current flow?
topics.answer: Counter-current flow maintains a nearly uniform temperature gradient along the entire heat exchanger, maximizing the log mean temperature difference (LMTD) and allowing the cold stream to be heated above the hot stream outlet temperature.

topics.question: What is the theoretical maximum thermal efficiency in a co-current heat exchanger with equal heat capacity rates?
topics.answer: In co-current flow with equal heat capacity rates (C_h = C_c), the maximum attainable effectiveness is 50%, because the two streams reach an identical equilibrium temperature at infinite length.

topics.question: How is the hydraulic diameter D_h calculated for the annular space of a double-pipe exchanger?
topics.answer: For an annulus between outer pipe inner diameter D_2 and inner pipe outer diameter D_1, wetted perimeter is π(D_2 + D_1) and area is π(D_2^2 - D_1^2)/4; hydraulic diameter is D_h = 4 A / P_w = D_2 - D_1.

topics.question: What is fouling resistance and how does it develop in double-pipe heat exchangers?
topics.answer: Fouling is the accumulation of mineral scale, biological slime, or corrosion products on tube walls, introducing an additional conductive resistance that degrades overall heat transfer over time.

topics.question: How does inner tube material thermal conductivity impact overall heat transfer coefficient U?
topics.answer: High-conductivity metals (e.g., copper k ≈ 390 W/(m·K)) minimize wall conductive resistance to negligible levels (< 1% of total), ensuring convective boundary layers govern thermal resistance.

topics.question: When are double-pipe heat exchangers preferred over shell-and-tube units in industry?
topics.answer: They are preferred for small duty applications (area < 20 m^2), high-pressure process streams (easier to contain in small-diameter pipes), and when true counter-current performance without F_T penalties is essential.

theory:
1. Concentric Double-Pipe Heat Exchanger Mechanics

The concentric double-pipe heat exchanger represents the canonical geometry for analyzing convective heat transfer in chemical processing. Consisting of two nested coaxial pipes, the design permits pure co-current or pure counter-current flow with zero crossflow mixing or baffle bypass.

2. First Law Enthalpy Balance & Heat Transfer Rate

Assuming adiabatic outer boundaries (negligible heat loss to ambient air), steady state, and constant fluid specific heat capacities $c_{p,h}$ and $c_{p,c}$, the thermal duty $q$ transferred from the inner hot stream to the annular cold stream is:

\[ q = \dot{m}_h c_{p,h} (T_{h,in} - T_{h,out}) = \dot{m}_c c_{p,c} (T_{c,out} - T_{c,in}) \]

where $\dot{m} = \rho V$ is mass flow rate. The overall heat transfer rate is governed by Newton's cooling law:

\[ q = U A \Delta T_{lm} \]

where $A = \pi D_o L$ is the outer surface area of the inner pipe and $\Delta T_{lm}$ is the log mean temperature difference.

3. Comparison of Co-Current vs Counter-Current Regimes

The terminal temperature differences for the two configurations are defined as:

  • Counter-Current Flow: $\Delta T_1 = T_{h,in} - T_{c,out}$ and $\Delta T_2 = T_{h,out} - T_{c,in}$. The temperature profiles slope in opposite directions, preventing local pinch bottlenecks and maximizing $\Delta T_{lm}$.
  • Co-Current Flow: $\Delta T_1 = T_{h,in} - T_{c,in}$ and $\Delta T_2 = T_{h,out} - T_{c,out}$. The driving force decreases rapidly along the tube, and cold fluid temperature cannot exceed hot outlet temperature.

4. Annular Flow Heat Transfer & Sensitivity Model

In the outer annular space, the hydraulic diameter is $D_h = D_2 - D_1$. Increasing cooling water flow rate $V_c$ elevates annular fluid velocity, thinning the laminar thermal boundary layer on the outer surface of the copper pipe. Over the operational flow envelope, counter-current thermal duty $q$ scales linearly with cooling water flow rate $V_c$:

\[ q = S \cdot V_c \]

where $S$ is the thermal duty flow sensitivity slope in $\text{kW/(L/min)}$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation determines the thermal duty $q$ and compares counter-current versus co-current performance in a copper-PVC concentric double-pipe heat exchanger ($L = 2.00\text{ m}$, $A = 0.1068\text{ m}^2$). With hot water circulating through the inner tube ($10.0\text{ L/min}$ at $60.0^\circ\text{C}$), cooling water flow rate $V_c$ in the outer annulus is stepped from $3.0$ to $18.0\text{ L/min}$ ($15.0^\circ\text{C}$ inlet) to determine the thermal duty slope $S = 0.4200\text{ kW/(L/min)}$ and verify counter-current superiority.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Thermal duty obeys enthalpy balance conservation: $q = \dot{m}_c c_{p,c} (T_{c,out} - T_{c,in})$. In the counter-current regime, thermal duty scales directly with cooling water throughput:

\[ q = S \cdot V_c \]

where $S = 0.4200\text{ kW/(L/min)}$ represents the experimental flow sensitivity slope. Overall heat transfer coefficient is evaluated via $U = q / (A \Delta T_{lm})$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The exchanger consists of a smooth drawn copper inner tube (ID $15.0\text{ mm}$, OD $17.0\text{ mm}$, length $2.00\text{ m}$, outer area $A = 0.1068\text{ m}^2$, $k = 385\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$) housed inside a transparent PVC outer shell (ID $28.0\text{ mm}$, annulus hydraulic diameter $D_h = 11.0\text{ mm}$). Four calibrated Pt100 RTD probes (accuracy $\pm 0.05^\circ\text{C}$) measure terminal stream temperatures. Cooling flow is metered by a precision rotameter (accuracy $\pm 0.1\text{ L/min}$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The valve manifold was aligned for counter-current flow. Hot water flow was fixed at $10.0\text{ L/min}$ at $60.00^\circ\text{C}$. Cooling water flow was set to $V_c = 3.0\text{ L/min}$ ($15.00^\circ\text{C}$ inlet). After 5 minutes of steady operation, all terminal temperatures were logged. Cooling flow was increased through $6.0, 9.0, 12.0, 15.0,$ and $18.0\text{ L/min}$, taking duplicate readings at each steady plateau.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Hot water circulation at $60^\circ\text{C}$ requires thermal burn precautions. Flexible hoses were reinforced with stainless steel braiding. Safety glasses, lab coats, and thermal gloves were worn during valve manipulations.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following measurements were recorded at constant inner-tube hot water flow $V_h = 10.0\text{ L/min}$ ($T_{h,in} = 60.00^\circ\text{C}$, $T_{c,in} = 15.00^\circ\text{C}$):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of counter-current thermal duty $q$ versus cooling water flow rate $V_c$ yields:

\[ q = 0.42000 \cdot V_c + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental slope $S = 0.42000\text{ kW/(L/min)}$ matches the reference target ($0.4200$) with $0.00\%$ deviation. Thermal duty expanded from $1.260\text{ kW}$ at $3\text{ L/min}$ to $7.560\text{ kW}$ at $18\text{ L/min}$.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainty in RTD temperature measurements is $\pm 0.05\text{ K}$, and rotameter flow uncertainty is $\pm 0.1\text{ L/min}$. Heat balance closure averaged $1.5\%$. Propagating errors yields an experimental uncertainty in thermal duty slope of $\pm 1.2\%$, reporting $S = 0.4200 \pm 0.0050\text{ kW/(L/min)}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The counter-current configuration demonstrated superior heat recovery. As cooling flow rate increased from $3.0$ to $18.0\text{ L/min}$, annular turbulence intensified, increasing the overall heat transfer coefficient from $291.9$ to $2242.4\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)}$. In co-current comparison runs, thermal duty plateaued prematurely due to the thermodynamic constraint $T_{c,out} \le T_{h,out}$.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Concentric pipe exchangers (hairpin exchangers) are widely deployed in petrochemical plants for high-pressure gas cooling, slurry heating, and viscous oil heat transfer. Standard modular hairpin banks allow flexible series/parallel reconfigurations as plant capacity expands.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is copper preferred over carbon steel for the inner tube in pilot-scale exchangers?
A1: Copper possesses high thermal conductivity ($k \approx 385\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$ vs $50\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$ for carbon steel) and excellent corrosion resistance in water service, eliminating tube wall resistance and fouling in laboratory teaching rigs.

Q2: What happens to the LMTD if both streams have identical heat capacity rates ($C_h = C_c$)?
A2: In counter-current flow, the temperature difference $\Delta T = T_h - T_c$ remains strictly constant throughout the length ($\Delta T_1 = \Delta T_2$); LMTD mathematically reduces to the simple arithmetic difference $\Delta T$.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The experiment verified heat transfer principles in a double-pipe concentric exchanger. The calibrated thermal duty sensitivity $S = 0.4200\text{ kW/(L/min)}$ ($q = 0.4200 \cdot V_c$) confirmed counter-current thermodynamic superiority and turbulent convective transport.

title: Plate-and-Frame Heat Exchanger Thermal Performance & Chevron Corrugation Conductance
aim: Determine the overall heat transfer coefficient U and thermal effectiveness of a gasketed plate-and-frame heat exchanger as a function of process stream velocity, evaluating the chevron corrugation enhancement factor.
intro: In food processing, pharmaceuticals, biochemical manufacturing, and specialty chemical synthesis, gasketed plate-and-frame heat exchangers (PHEs) have largely superseded traditional shell-and-tube units for low-to-medium pressure duties. A plate heat exchanger consists of a pack of corrugated thin stainless steel or titanium plates compressed between a fixed head and movable follower frame. Elastomeric gaskets seal the plate perimeters and direct hot and cold fluids into alternate narrow inter-plate channels in true counter-current flow. The defining feature of PHEs is the chevron (herringbone) surface corrugation pressed into each plate. Adjacent plates are inverted so that corrugation ridges cross, forming a complex three-dimensional network of intersecting tortuous channels. These corrugations induce continuous swirling vortex shedding and boundary layer disruption at Reynolds numbers as low as 50 to 100, transitioning into intense turbulence well below the Re = 2,300 threshold of smooth tubes. Consequently, plate heat exchangers achieve exceptionally high overall heat transfer coefficients U (often 3 to 5 times greater than tubular exchangers), allowing extremely close temperature approaches (less than 1 °C) and compact footprints. In this experiment, an instrumented 10-plate chevron heat exchanger is operated across channel velocities from 0.10 to 0.60 m/s to quantify overall conductance U and verify empirical power-law velocity scaling U = S · v_p^0.65.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 10-plate stainless steel PHE (plate width 100 mm, length 300 mm, chevron angle β = 60°, total active area A = 0.240 m^2). Linear regression models U versus (v_p)^0.65.

topics.question: How do chevron corrugations promote turbulence at exceptionally low Reynolds numbers?
topics.answer: The crossing corrugations force fluid to split, swirl, and recombine continuously in three-dimensional helical vortices, destroying laminar boundary layers and inducing turbulent mixing at Reynolds numbers as low as Re = 50 to 100.

topics.question: What is the trade-off between thermal enhancement and hydraulic pressure drop in PHEs?
topics.answer: The intense swirling vortex generation that elevates heat transfer coefficients by 300% to 500% also creates high form drag and friction, producing substantially higher pressure drops per unit length than smooth tubes.

topics.question: What is the significance of the chevron angle β (typically 30° vs 60°)?
topics.answer: A 30° chevron (low-theta) plate produces lower pressure drop and moderate heat transfer; a 60° chevron (high-theta) plate generates intense turbulence and high heat transfer coefficients at the expense of higher pumping head.

topics.question: Why can plate heat exchangers achieve very close temperature approaches (< 1 °C)?
topics.answer: The high overall heat transfer coefficient U, true counter-current flow without crossflow bypass, and high thermal length (NTU) allow cold fluid to approach hot fluid inlet temperature within fractions of a degree.

topics.question: How are plate heat exchangers cleaned in food and pharmaceutical manufacturing?
topics.answer: They are cleaned in place (CIP) by circulating caustic detergent and acid sanitizing solutions at high velocity, or dismantled rapidly by loosening compression bolts for manual inspection and sanitization.

topics.question: What are the primary operating limits of gasketed plate heat exchangers?
topics.answer: Elastomeric gaskets (nitrile, EPDM, Viton) limit operating temperatures to typically < 160 °C and pressures to < 25 bar; exceeding these limits requires welded or brazed plate designs.

quiz.question: In a plate heat exchanger, turbulent flow is typically initiated at Reynolds numbers around:
quiz.explanation: Chevron corrugations disrupt boundary layers so aggressively that flow becomes fully turbulent at Reynolds numbers as low as 50 to 100.

quiz.question: The main mechanical component limiting the operating temperature and pressure of a gasketed PHE is:
quiz.explanation: Elastomeric gaskets degrade and soften at elevated temperatures (> 160 °C) and can blow out under high pressure (> 25 bar).

quiz.question: A chevron corrugation angle of 60° (high-theta plate) compared to 30° provides:
options: Lower heat transfer and lower pressure drop
Higher heat transfer and higher pressure drop
quiz.explanation: Steeper chevron angles force fluid into more severe transverse zigzag paths, enhancing heat transfer at the expense of substantially higher pressure drop.

theory:
1. Architecture of Gasketed Plate Heat Exchangers

Plate-and-frame heat exchangers (PHEs) provide compact, high-efficiency thermal processing across food, bioprocess, and chemical industries. Thin, corrugated metal plates ($0.5$ to $0.8\text{ mm}$ thickness) are clamped together in a frame, with elastomeric perimeter gaskets sealing alternate channels to establish isolated hot and cold counter-current flow paths.

2. Chevron Corrugation Hydrodynamics & Heat Transfer Enhancement

The characteristic herringbone (chevron) pattern pressed into each plate induces three-dimensional swirling vortices that continuously renew the thermal boundary layer. In conventional smooth conduits, laminar-to-turbulent transition occurs at $Re \approx 2,300$. In chevron plates, transition occurs at $Re \approx 50$ to $100$. The Nusselt number in corrugated plate channels is modeled by the Martin / Heavner empirical power-law correlation:

\[ Nu = \frac{h D_h}{k} = C \cdot Re^m Pr^n \]

where $D_h = 2 b$ is the hydraulic diameter ($b$ is mean channel corrugation depth, typically $2$ to $4\text{ mm}$) and exponent $m$ typically ranges from $0.65$ to $0.70$ for $60^\circ$ chevron angles.

3. Overall Conductance Model

Because the plates are extremely thin ($0.6\text{ mm}$) and manufactured from high-grade 316 stainless steel ($k = 16\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$), wall conductive resistance is minimal ($R_{wall} = t / k \approx 3.75 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^2\cdot\text{K/W}$). When operating in turbulent liquid-liquid service, convective film coefficients $h_h$ and $h_c$ govern performance. Relating overall heat transfer coefficient $U$ to process channel velocity $v_p$:

\[ U = S \cdot (v_p)^{0.65} \]

where $S$ is the plate exchanger conductance coefficient in $\text{W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.65}$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation evaluates the thermal performance of an industrial gasketed plate-and-frame heat exchanger ($10\text{ plates}$, total heat transfer area $A = 0.240\text{ m}^2$, $60^\circ$ chevron corrugation). By measuring terminal temperatures and pressure drops across process channel velocities from $0.10$ to $0.60\text{ m/s}$ at constant cold utility conditions ($10.0\text{ L/min}$ at $15.0^\circ\text{C}$), we evaluate overall heat transfer coefficient $U$, verify the $v_p^{0.65}$ empirical scaling model, and determine the conductance coefficient $S = 3200.0000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.65}$.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Thermal duty is calculated from hot process stream enthalpy drop: $q = \dot{m}_h c_{p,h} (T_{h,in} - T_{h,out})$. Overall heat transfer coefficient $U$ is computed via $U = q / (A \Delta T_{lm})$, where $\Delta T_{lm}$ is pure counter-current LMTD. The scaling model follows:

\[ U = S \cdot (v_p)^{0.65} \]

where $S = 3200.0000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.65}$ is the characteristic chevron conductance slope.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The unit features 10 corrugated type 316 stainless steel plates (plate width $100\text{ mm}$, length $300\text{ mm}$, thickness $0.6\text{ mm}$, corrugation amplitude $b = 2.5\text{ mm}$, chevron angle $\beta = 60^\circ$, active area $A = 0.240\text{ m}^2$) sealed with food-grade EPDM gaskets. Four Pt100 RTDs (accuracy $\pm 0.02^\circ\text{C}$) log terminal temperatures. Process flow is metered by a magnetic inductive flowmeter (accuracy $\pm 0.2\%$). Differential pressure across plate channels is recorded by a piezoresistive transmitter ($0\text{--}100\text{ kPa}$, accuracy $\pm 0.05\%$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The plate pack tightening dimension was verified at $32.0\text{ mm}$. The unit was preheated with hot water at $55.00^\circ\text{C}$ and cold water at $15.00^\circ\text{C}$. Cold utility flow was fixed at $10.0\text{ L/min}$. Process velocity was set to $v_p = 0.10\text{ m/s}$ ($V_h = 1.50\text{ L/min}$ across 5 hot channels). After 120 seconds of thermal steady state, all four temperatures and channel pressure drops were logged. Velocity was stepped through $0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50,$ and $0.60\text{ m/s}$.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

High clamping force on the plate pack requires strict adherence to tightening specifications to avoid plate warping. Hot water at $55^\circ\text{C}$ was contained within pressure-rated piping. Safety glasses, lab coats, and protective gloves were worn.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following observations were recorded at constant cold utility flow $V_c = 10.0\text{ L/min}$ ($T_{c,in} = 15.00^\circ\text{C}$, $T_{h,in} = 55.00^\circ\text{C}$):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of overall heat transfer coefficient $U$ versus $(v_p)^{0.65}$ yields:

\[ U = 3200.00000 \cdot (v_p)^{0.65} + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental slope $S = 3200.0000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.65}$ exactly matches the calibration target ($3200.0000$). At $v_p = 0.60\text{ m/s}$, the overall coefficient reached $U = 2283.3\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)}$, over three times higher than smooth tubular exchangers at comparable velocities.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainty in RTD temperature measurements is $\pm 0.02\text{ K}$, and flowmeter uncertainty is $\pm 0.2\%$. Heat balance closure across all runs averaged $1.1\%$. Propagating errors yields an experimental uncertainty in $U$ of $\pm 0.95\%$, reporting $S = 3200.0000 \pm 30.4\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.65}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The remarkable heat transfer coefficients observed in this plate exchanger stem from the $60^\circ$ chevron corrugation. The high shear rate developed at the corrugation peaks disrupts the laminar sublayer, preventing stagnant boundary layer growth. The close temperature approach ($T_{h,out} - T_{c,in} = 10.35\text{ K}$ at low velocity) demonstrates the high thermal effectiveness characteristic of PHE units.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Plate heat exchangers are standard in pasteurization, dairy processing, brewing, and modular chemical skid systems. Their compact volume-to-area ratio ($> 1000\text{ m}^2/\text{m}^3$) saves plant floor space, and plates can be easily added or removed to modify plant thermal duty.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is thermal length ($\Theta = \Delta T / \Delta T_{lm} = ext{NTU}$) a key design parameter for plate exchangers?
A1: Thermal length characterizes the temperature change achieved per unit driving force; high-theta plates achieve large temperature spans in a single pass, whereas low-theta plates handle high volumetric flow rates with lower pressure drop.

Q2: What is the main cause of fouling in plate heat exchangers?
A2: Fibrous particulate matter or debris in raw cooling water can bridge the narrow inter-plate gap ($2\text{--}4\text{ mm}$), blocking channels and causing localized flow maldistribution; upstream basket strainers ($< 0.5\text{ mm}$ mesh) are mandatory.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The plate-and-frame heat exchanger demonstrated superior convective transport. The measured conductance scaling slope $S = 3200.0000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.65}$ ($U = 3200.0000 \cdot v_p^{0.65}$) verified high-performance chevron vortex hydrodynamics for chemical process operations.

title: Extended Surface Heat Transfer & Forced Convection Over Finned Cylinders
aim: Measure convective heat dissipation from an electrically heated cylinder equipped with extended longitudinal fins in a low-speed wind tunnel, determine convective coefficient h as a function of air crossflow velocity, and evaluate fin efficiency η_f.
intro: In chemical process cooling towers, air-cooled condensers, reboilers, and electronic heat sinks, transferring heat to or from gases represents a severe transport bottleneck because gases possess low thermal conductivities and low heat capacities. Consequently, the gas-side convective heat transfer coefficient h is typically 10 to 50 times lower than liquid-side coefficients, dominating the overall thermal resistance. To compensate for this limitation, extended surfaces (fins) are bonded, extruded, or machined onto the gas-contacting perimeter, dramatically multiplying the effective heat transfer surface area. However, heat must conduct along the fin from the base to the tip while simultaneously dissipating convectively into the crossflow air stream. This continuous thermal dissipation causes a longitudinal temperature drop along the fin, meaning the fin surface operates at a lower average temperature than the bare cylinder base. This performance reduction is quantified by the fin efficiency η_f, defined as the actual heat dissipated by the fin divided by the ideal heat that would be dissipated if the entire fin remained at the base temperature T_b: η_f = tanh(m L_c) / (m L_c), where m = sqrt(2 h / (k t)). In crossflow forced convection, the convective coefficient h scales with free-stream velocity v_inf to the 0.6 power (Hilpert / Churchill–Bernstein correlation). In this laboratory investigation, an electrically heated aluminum finned cylinder is tested in a benchtop wind tunnel across air velocities from 1.0 to 6.0 m/s to determine the convective scaling slope S and evaluate fin efficiency.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 50.0 mm diameter aluminum cylinder with 12 radial longitudinal fins (length L = 25.0 mm, thickness t = 2.0 mm, total extended area A_tot = 0.185 m^2). Linear regression models h versus (v_inf)^0.6.

topics.question: What is the physical significance of fin efficiency η_f and why is it always less than 1.0?
topics.answer: Fin efficiency is the ratio of actual heat dissipated by the fin to the ideal heat that would be dissipated if the entire fin were isothermal at the base temperature; finite thermal conductivity k creates a temperature gradient along the fin length, ensuring η_f < 1.0.

topics.question: How does the fin parameter m = sqrt(2 h / (k t)) govern temperature distribution along a fin?
topics.answer: The parameter m represents the ratio of convective surface conductance to conductive longitudinal resistance; a larger m (low k, thin fin, or high h) produces a steep temperature drop and low fin efficiency.

topics.question: Why are extended surfaces almost exclusively installed on the gas side rather than liquid side?
topics.answer: Gases have very low convective coefficients (h ≈ 10–100 W/(m^2·K)) compared to liquids (h ≈ 1,000–10,000 W/(m^2·K)); adding fins to the gas side balances the thermal resistances and provides maximum overall heat duty improvement.

topics.question: What is fin effectiveness ε_f and how does it differ from fin efficiency η_f?
topics.answer: Fin efficiency η_f compares actual fin heat transfer to ideal isothermal fin heat transfer; fin effectiveness ε_f is the ratio of heat transferred with the fin to heat transferred from the bare base area without the fin (fins are justified only if ε_f > 2).

topics.question: Why does aluminum remain the dominant material for finned heat exchangers despite copper having higher conductivity?
topics.answer: While copper has higher conductivity (400 vs 205 W/(m·K)), aluminum has one-third the density, is significantly cheaper, easier to extrude into complex fin profiles, and provides superior heat transfer per unit mass and cost.

topics.question: How does radiation heat transfer contribute to total heat dissipation from a finned cylinder?
topics.answer: At moderate base temperatures (< 100 °C), radiative dissipation to ambient surroundings typically accounts for 5% to 10% of total heat loss, calculated via q_rad = ε_emissivity σ A_tot (T_b^4 - T_surr^4).

quiz.question: For forced convection heat transfer across a cylinder in crossflow, the convective coefficient h typically scales with velocity as:
quiz.explanation: Classical empirical correlations for crossflow over tube banks (such as Hilpert or Zukauskas) establish Nu ∝ Re^0.6, meaning h scales with v^0.6.

quiz.question: The efficiency η_f of a straight rectangular fin of length L with an insulated tip is given by:
quiz.explanation: Exact one-dimensional analytical solution of the steady fin conduction equation yields η_f = tanh(m L) / (m L), where m = sqrt(2 h / (k t)).

quiz.question: Adding fins to a heat transfer surface is thermally justifiable only if fin effectiveness ε_f is:
quiz.explanation: If ε_f < 1, the fin acts as an insulator; engineering standards require ε_f > 2.0 to justify the added weight, material expense, and pressure drop.

quiz.question: If the thermal conductivity k of a fin material is doubled, the fin parameter m = sqrt(2 h / (k t)) will:
options: Decrease by a factor of sqrt(2)
quiz.explanation: Because k is in the denominator under the square root, doubling k decreases m by a factor of sqrt(2) ≈ 1.414, flattening the temperature gradient and increasing fin efficiency.

measureLabel: Record finned cylinder convective heat transfer
theory:
1. Extended Surface Principles & Biot Number Criterion

In thermal process engineering, transferring heat between a solid boundary and a flowing gas presents a substantial transport barrier due to low gas-side convective coefficients ($h \approx 10\text{--}100\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)}$). Installing extended surfaces (fins) increases total exposed area $A_{tot}$, mitigating this resistance.

For a thin fin of thickness $t$, length $L$, and thermal conductivity $k$, the transverse Biot number $Bi = h (t/2) / k \ll 0.1$, justifying the classical one-dimensional conduction approximation along coordinate $x$ from base ($x = 0$) to tip ($x = L$).

2. The One-Dimensional Fin Equation

An energy balance on an infinitesimal fin element $dx$ under steady state yields:

\[ \frac{d^2 T}{dx^2} - \frac{h P}{k A_c} (T - T_\infty) = 0 \implies \frac{d^2 \theta}{dx^2} - m^2 \theta = 0 \]

where $\theta(x) = T(x) - T_\infty$, $P$ is fin perimeter, $A_c$ is cross-sectional area, and $m = \sqrt{\frac{h P}{k A_c}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{2 h}{k t}}$ for a thin rectangular fin ($P \approx 2W$, $A_c = W t$).

3. Fin Efficiency & Total Heat Dissipation

Applying the convective tip boundary condition (or insulated tip with corrected length $L_c = L + t/2$):

\[ \eta_f = \frac{q_{actual}}{q_{ideal}} = \frac{\tanh(m L_c)}{m L_c} \]

The total heat dissipated from an array of $N$ fins sharing base area $A_b$ is:

\[ q_{tot} = h \eta_o A_{tot} (T_b - T_\infty) \]

where $\eta_o = 1 - \frac{N A_f}{A_{tot}} (1 - \eta_f)$ is overall surface efficiency. In crossflow forced convection, the convective coefficient $h$ scales with free-stream air velocity $v_\infty$ via the Hilpert correlation ($Nu = C Re^{0.6} Pr^{0.33}$):

\[ h = S \cdot (v_\infty)^{0.6} \]

where $S$ is the forced convection scaling slope in $\text{W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.6}$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation determines the convective heat transfer coefficient $h$ and fin efficiency $\eta_f$ for an aluminum finned cylinder ($12\text{ longitudinal fins}$, total area $A_{tot} = 0.185\text{ m}^2$, $k = 205\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$) placed in a low-speed wind tunnel. Across air crossflow velocities from $1.0$ to $6.0\text{ m/s}$ at constant electrical heat input $Q_e = 150.0\text{ W}$, we verify the $v_\infty^{0.6}$ scaling law, evaluate the convective coefficient slope $S = 18.5000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.6}$, and track fin efficiency $\eta_f$.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Total heat dissipated by the finned cylinder is $q = Q_e - q_{rad} = h A_{eff} (T_b - T_\infty)$, where $A_{eff} = \eta_o A_{tot}$. The convective heat transfer coefficient is evaluated as:

\[ h = S \cdot (v_\infty)^{0.6} \]

where $S = 18.5000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.6}$ represents the empirical forced convection scaling factor. Fin efficiency is computed via $\eta_f = \tanh(m L_c) / (m L_c)$ with $m = \sqrt{2 h / (k t)}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The test assembly comprises a $50.0\text{ mm}$ outer diameter 6061-T6 aluminum cylinder ($k = 205\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$) with 12 radial longitudinal fins (length $L = 25.0\text{ mm}$, thickness $t = 2.0\text{ mm}$, axial span $150\text{ mm}$, total area $A_{tot} = 0.1850\text{ m}^2$) mounted across a $200\text{ mm} \times 200\text{ mm}$ wind tunnel test section. An internal cartridge heater delivers $150.0\text{ W}$. Temperatures are monitored by calibrated miniature Type K thermocouples (accuracy $\pm 0.1^\circ\text{C}$). Air velocity is measured by a hot-wire anemometer (accuracy $\pm 0.05\text{ m/s}$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The cylinder was centered in the wind tunnel and the heater energized at $Q_e = 150.0\text{ W}$. Approach air velocity was adjusted to $v_\infty = 1.0\text{ m/s}$. The system was allowed 20 minutes to achieve thermal equilibrium (temperature drift $< 0.1^\circ\text{C/min}$). Cylinder base temperature $T_b$, fin tip temperature $T_{tip}$, air temperature $T_\infty$, and heater wattage were logged. Air velocity was stepped through $2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0,$ and $6.0\text{ m/s}$.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

The aluminum cylinder reaches elevated temperatures ($> 80^\circ\text{C}$) during testing, presenting thermal contact burn hazards. Protective thermal gloves and lab coats were worn. The heater was interlocked with the wind tunnel fan to prevent uncooled thermal runaway.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following measurements were recorded at constant electrical power $Q_e = 150.0\text{ W}$ and ambient air temperature $T_\infty = 20.0^\circ\text{C}$:
