7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of convective heat transfer coefficient $h$ versus $(v_\infty)^{0.6}$ yields:

\[ h = 18.50000 \cdot (v_\infty)^{0.6} + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental slope $S = 18.5000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.6}$ matches the calibration benchmark ($18.5000$) with $0.00\%$ deviation. As velocity increased from $1.0$ to $6.0\text{ m/s}$, the base temperature dropped from $68.22^\circ\text{C}$ to $39.11^\circ\text{C}$, while fin efficiency remained high ($\eta_f = 0.942$ to $0.851$).

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainty in thermocouple readings is $\pm 0.1\text{ K}$, power measurement uncertainty is $\pm 0.1\text{ W}$, and hot-wire anemometer uncertainty is $\pm 0.05\text{ m/s}$. Propagating into $h$ yields an overall experimental uncertainty of $\pm 1.3\%$, reporting $S = 18.5000 \pm 0.24\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.6}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The excellent agreement with the $v_\infty^{0.6}$ power law confirms crossflow boundary layer thinning over the fin array. The high thermal conductivity of aluminum ($205\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$) ensures that fin efficiency remains above $85\%$ even at the highest air velocity ($6.0\text{ m/s}$), proving that the fin thickness ($2.0\text{ mm}$) and length ($25.0\text{ mm}$) are well-proportioned.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Finned cylinders are the core heat transfer geometry in air-cooled heat exchangers (fin-fan coolers) in arid petrochemical refineries, compressor intercoolers, and HVAC heat pumps. Selecting the optimal fin density and thickness balances manufacturing cost against aerodynamic air-side pressure drop.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does fin efficiency decrease as air velocity increases?
A1: Higher air velocity increases the convective heat transfer coefficient $h$, increasing the fin parameter $m = \sqrt{2 h / (k t)}$. A larger $m$ produces a steeper temperature drop along the fin, reducing the average fin temperature relative to the base and lowering $\eta_f$.

Q2: What is the risk of placing fins too close together on a cylinder?
A2: If fin spacing is smaller than the boundary layer thickness ($2 \delta$), thermal boundary layers from adjacent fins merge, choking airflow through the channels and severely degrading heat transfer.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The extended surface forced convection experiment confirmed the Hilpert crossflow power law. The verified scaling slope $S = 18.5000\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)/(m/s)}^{0.6}$ ($h = 18.5000 \cdot v_\infty^{0.6}$) validated fin conduction-convection dynamics for chemical process heat exchanger design.

title: Radial Steady-State Conduction & Thermal Conductivity of Process Insulation
aim: Measure the steady-state radial temperature distribution across a cylindrical specimen of process insulation material under controlled electrical heating, verify Fourier's law in cylindrical coordinates, and determine thermal conductivity k.
yAxis: Radial temperature difference ΔT = T_1 - T_2 (K)
intro: In chemical process plants, cryogenic storage terminals, and steam distribution systems, thermal insulation materials—such as calcium silicate, mineral wool, expanded perlite, and cellular glass—are mandatory to minimize parasitic thermal losses, prevent personnel burn injuries, avoid pipeline freezing, and suppress condensation. Determining the thermal conductivity k of tubular process insulation is vital for accurate thermal design. In cylindrical geometries, heat flows radially outward from an internal coaxial heating element through an annular insulation sleeve of inner radius r_1, outer radius r_2, and length L. Applying Fourier's fundamental law of heat conduction in one-dimensional steady cylindrical coordinates yields: q_r = -k A(r) · (dT/dr) = -k (2π r L) · (dT/dr). Separating variables and integrating across the annular wall establishes the classic logarithmic temperature profile: T(r) = T_1 - (T_1 - T_2) · [ln(r/r_1) / ln(r_2/r_1)], and gives the steady radial heat flow rate: q_r = [2π k L / ln(r_2/r_1)] · (T_1 - T_2). In this laboratory experiment, an annular specimen of refractory process insulation is heated with an internal coaxial electrical element across power levels from 20 to 120 W with guarded end heaters to eliminate axial heat leakage. Measuring the radial temperature difference ΔT = T_1 - T_2 directly evaluates the thermal resistance slope S and determines the material thermal conductivity k.
modelExtra: Evaluated using an insulation test sleeve (inner radius r_1 = 20.0 mm, outer radius r_2 = 50.0 mm, effective length L = 500 mm). Linear regression models ΔT versus electric power Q_e to extract thermal conductivity k = 0.1450 W/(m·K).

topics.question: Why does the temperature profile in a cylinder vary logarithmically rather than linearly as in a flat slab?
topics.answer: In cylindrical coordinates, the heat conduction area A(r) = 2π r L expands continuously with increasing radius; to maintain constant total heat flux q_r, the temperature gradient dT/dr must decrease inversely with radius (dT/dr ∝ 1/r), integrating to a logarithmic curve.

topics.question: What is the critical radius of insulation r_cr and why is it vital for pipe insulation design?
topics.answer: The critical radius r_cr = k / h is the outer insulation radius at which total thermal resistance is minimized; adding insulation to a pipe with radius r_o < r_cr actually increases heat loss because surface area expansion outweighs conductive insulation resistance.

topics.question: How do active guard heaters prevent experimental measurement error in radial conduction apparatus?
topics.answer: Guard heaters at cylinder ends are maintained at identical temperatures to the central core, driving axial temperature gradients to zero (dT/dz = 0) and ensuring 100% of electrical power dissipates purely radially.

topics.question: How does moisture ingress degrade the performance of industrial thermal insulation?
topics.answer: Water has a thermal conductivity (k ≈ 0.6 W/(m·K)) more than an order of magnitude higher than dry air (k ≈ 0.026 W/(m·K)) trapped in insulation pores; moisture filling pores drastically increases effective conductivity and accelerates corrosion under insulation (CUI).

topics.question: What mechanisms of heat transfer operate inside porous insulation materials?
topics.answer: Apparent thermal conductivity combines solid matrix conduction, pore gas conduction, natural convection within micro-pores (negligible for pore diameter < 1 mm), and radiative radiation between pore walls.

topics.question: What is the economic thickness of insulation (ETI) in process engineering?
topics.answer: ETI is the insulation thickness that minimizes total annualized cost, balancing the annualized capital cost of insulation against the monetary value of saved thermal energy over the facility lifetime.

precautions: Allow sufficient equilibration time (30 to 45 minutes) between power changes, as insulating materials have very low thermal diffusivity.

quiz.question: The critical radius of insulation for a circular pipe exposed to convection is given by:
quiz.explanation: Differentiating total thermal resistance with respect to outer radius and setting to zero yields r_cr = k / h.

quiz.question: If the outer radius of an insulated pipe is smaller than the critical radius (r_o < r_cr), adding more insulation will:
options: Cool the pipe below ambient temperature
quiz.explanation: When r_o < r_cr, the increase in external convective surface area has a greater thermal impact than added conductive resistance, causing net heat loss to rise.

quiz.question: Guarded end heaters in radial conductivity apparatus are used to enforce the condition:
options: Axial temperature gradient dT/dz is zero
quiz.explanation: By heating the cylinder ends to the core temperature, the axial gradient is eliminated (dT/dz = 0), forcing all heat to conduct strictly radially.

theory:
1. Fourier's Law in Cylindrical Coordinates

Thermal insulation in chemical plants protects piping, reactors, and distillation columns from energy loss. Analysis of thermal conduction through cylindrical pipe walls requires Fourier's law expressed in cylindrical coordinates $(r, \theta, z)$. Assuming steady state, one-dimensional radial heat flow, and constant thermal conductivity $k$:

\[ q_r = -k A(r) \frac{dT}{dr} = -k (2\pi r L) \frac{dT}{dr} \]

where $A(r) = 2\pi r L$ is the isothermal cylindrical surface area at radius $r$.

2. Integration of Radial Conduction Equation

Separating variables and integrating between inner boundary ($r = r_1, T = T_1$) and outer boundary ($r = r_2, T = T_2$):

\[ \frac{q_r}{2\pi k L} \int_{r_1}^{r_2} \frac{dr}{r} = -\int_{T_1}^{T_2} dT \implies \frac{q_r}{2\pi k L} \ln\left( \frac{r_2}{r_1} \right) = T_1 - T_2 = \Delta T \]

Solving for temperature difference $\Delta T$ in terms of radial heat flow rate $q_r$:

\[ \Delta T = \left[ \frac{\ln(r_2 / r_1)}{2\pi k L} \right] q_r = R_{cyl} \cdot q_r \]

where $R_{cyl} = \frac{\ln(r_2 / r_1)}{2\pi k L}$ is the conductive thermal resistance of the cylindrical sleeve in $\text{K/W}$.

3. Measurement Model & Thermal Conductivity Evaluation

In an electrically heated apparatus with active guard heaters, axial losses are suppressed, meaning electrical power input $Q_e = V I$ equals radial conduction heat rate ($q_r = Q_e$). The linear model relating temperature difference $\Delta T$ to power $Q_e$ is:

\[ \Delta T = S \cdot Q_e \]

where $S$ is the experimental thermal resistance slope. From the known sleeve geometry ($r_1, r_2, L$), the thermal conductivity $k$ is directly evaluated as:

\[ k = \frac{\ln(r_2 / r_1)}{2\pi L \cdot S} \]
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation determines the thermal conductivity $k$ of a cylindrical specimen of industrial calcium silicate pipe insulation (inner radius $r_1 = 20.0\text{ mm}$, outer radius $r_2 = 50.0\text{ mm}$, active length $L = 500\text{ mm}$). By applying controlled electrical heating from $20.0$ to $120.0\text{ W}$ with guarded end heaters and logging the radial temperature difference $\Delta T = T_1 - T_2$, we verify Fourier's logarithmic conduction law, measure thermal resistance slope $S = 0.3850\text{ K/W}$, and determine material conductivity $k = 0.1450\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Radial heat conduction through a cylindrical sleeve obeys Fourier's law:

\[ \Delta T = T_1 - T_2 = \left[ \frac{\ln(r_2 / r_1)}{2\pi k L} \right] Q_e = S \cdot Q_e \]

where $S = 0.3850\text{ K/W}$ represents the cylindrical conductive thermal resistance. Thermal conductivity is computed via $k = \frac{\ln(r_2 / r_1)}{2\pi L S}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The apparatus features a central Nichrome cartridge heater ($D = 40.0\text{ mm}$, $r_1 = 20.0\text{ mm}$) fitted inside an insulation sleeve ($r_2 = 50.0\text{ mm}$, outer circumference $A_o = 0.1571\text{ m}^2$, length $L = 500\text{ mm}$) surrounded by a water-cooled copper jacket maintained at $T_2 = 25.0^\circ\text{C}$. Active guard heaters at both ends suppress axial heat leakage. Calibrated Type K thermocouples (accuracy $\pm 0.05^\circ\text{C}$) record inner, outer, and intermediate radial temperatures. Electrical power is supplied by a regulated DC power source (accuracy $\pm 0.05\text{ W}$).

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

Cooling water circulation was started at $5.0\text{ L/min}$. Guard heaters were energized and balanced to eliminate axial temperature gradients ($|T_{core} - T_{guard}| < 0.05^\circ\text{C}$). Core heater power was set to $Q_e = 20.0\text{ W}$. The system was allowed 45 minutes to achieve thermal steady state before recording $T_1$, $T_2$, and $\Delta T$. Heater power was stepped in increments of $20.0\text{ W}$ up to $120.0\text{ W}$, allowing full thermal equilibration at each level.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

The central core reaches high temperatures ($> 70^\circ\text{C}$). Protective thermal gloves and safety glasses were worn. Over-temperature limit switches were set to shut down heater power if core temperature exceeded $200^\circ\text{C}$.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following measurements were recorded at constant outer jacket temperature $T_2 = 25.00^\circ\text{C}$:

RunHeater Power $Q_e$ (W)Outer Temp $T_2$ (°C)Inner Temp $T_1$ (°C)Radial Diff $\Delta T$ (K)Conductivity $k$ (W/(m·K))
120.025.0032.707.700.1450
240.025.0040.4015.400.1450
360.025.0048.1023.100.1450
480.025.0055.8030.800.1450
5100.025.0063.5038.500.1450
6120.025.0071.2046.200.1450

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of radial temperature difference $\Delta T$ versus heater power $Q_e$ yields:

\[ \Delta T = 0.38500 \cdot Q_e + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. Using geometric parameters $r_1 = 0.020\text{ m}$, $r_2 = 0.050\text{ m}$, and $L = 0.500\text{ m}$:

\[ \ln(r_2 / r_1) = \ln(50.0 / 20.0) = \ln(2.5) = 0.91629 \]

Thermal conductivity is computed as:

\[ k = \frac{\ln(r_2 / r_1)}{2\pi L S} = \frac{0.91629}{2 \cdot \pi \cdot 0.500 \cdot 0.38500} = \frac{0.91629}{1.20951} = 0.1450\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)} \]

matching the engineering specification ($k = 0.1450\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$) with $0.00\%$ deviation.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Thermocouple accuracy is $\pm 0.05\text{ K}$, power measurement uncertainty is $\pm 0.05\text{ W}$, and radius measurement uncertainty is $\pm 0.1\text{ mm}$. Propagating errors yields an experimental uncertainty in thermal conductivity of $\pm 1.1\%$, reporting $k = 0.1450 \pm 0.0016\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The strictly linear relationship between $\Delta T$ and $Q_e$ confirms that thermal conductivity remains independent of temperature over the operating span ($25^\circ\text{C}$ to $71^\circ\text{C}$). The measured value ($0.1450\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$) is typical for industrial calcium silicate insulation, confirming effective pore structure and dry porous media performance.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Calcium silicate insulation is specified for high-temperature steam headers, cracking furnace transfer lines, and hot oil piping up to $650^\circ\text{C}$. Accurate conductivity values allow chemical engineers to calculate required insulation thickness to maintain surface temperatures below $60^\circ\text{C}$ for personnel burn protection (ASTM C1055).

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is calcium silicate preferred over glass fiber for high-temperature industrial steam lines?
A1: Calcium silicate provides superior compressive strength (can withstand foot traffic on insulated pipes without crushing) and retains structural integrity at temperatures up to $650^\circ\text{C}$, whereas organic binders in fiberglass burn out above $250^\circ\text{C}$.

Q2: How does corrosion under insulation (CUI) develop and how can it be detected?
A2: Water penetrates damaged weather jacketing and wicks through porous insulation, contacting carbon steel pipe walls in the presence of oxygen and dissolved salts; it is detected using pulsed eddy current testing or radiography without stripping insulation.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The experiment verified Fourier's radial conduction law in cylindrical coordinates. The measured thermal resistance slope $S = 0.3850\text{ K/W}$ established an exact thermal conductivity $k = 0.1450\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$ for the calcium silicate process insulation.

title: Unsteady-State Transient Conduction & Lumped Thermal Capacitance Cooling
aim: Study the transient quenching of solid metallic cylinders in an agitated water bath, verify the lumped thermal capacitance model (Biot number Bi < 0.1), and determine the convective cooling time constant τ and heat transfer coefficient h.
intro: In chemical process engineering, metallurgical heat treatment, polymer extrusion pelletizing, and food blanching, unsteady-state (transient) heat transfer dictates processing cycle times, microstructure evolution, and thermal stress generation. When a hot solid body is abruptly plunged into a cooler agitated fluid medium, heat conducts from the interior of the solid to its surface and is subsequently removed by convective boundary layer dissipation into the surrounding fluid. The governing thermal behavior depends critically on the relative magnitude of internal conduction resistance to external surface convective resistance, quantified by the dimensionless Biot number: Bi = h · L_c / k, where h is the convective heat transfer coefficient, k is solid thermal conductivity, and L_c = V / A_s is the characteristic body dimension. When Bi < 0.1, internal conductive resistance is negligible compared to surface convection, meaning temperature gradients within the solid remain virtually flat (spatially uniform temperature). Under this lumped thermal capacitance condition, the transient energy balance yields pure exponential decay: (T(t) - T_inf) / (T_0 - T_inf) = exp(-t / τ), where thermal time constant τ = (ρ · V · c_p) / (h · A_s) = 1 / k_rate. In this laboratory investigation, a brass test cylinder instrumented with centerline thermocouples is quenched from 85.0 °C into an agitated cooling bath to confirm lumped capacitance dynamics and evaluate the cooling decay rate k_rate.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a solid brass cylinder (diameter D = 25.0 mm, length L = 50.0 mm, density ρ = 8530 kg/m^3, specific heat c_p = 380 J/(kg·K), thermal conductivity k = 115 W/(m·K), Bi = 0.025). Linear regression models ln(θ/θ_0) versus t to extract k_rate = 0.0320 s^-1.

topics.question: What is the physical criterion for the validity of the lumped thermal capacitance model?
topics.answer: The Biot number must be less than 0.1 (Bi = h L_c / k < 0.1); this ensures internal conduction resistance is less than 10% of external convective resistance, keeping spatial temperature variations within the solid below 5%.

topics.question: What is the characteristic length L_c for a solid body in lumped capacitance analysis?
topics.answer: Characteristic length is defined as body volume divided by external surface area (L_c = V / A_s); for a sphere L_c = r_o / 3, and for an infinitely long cylinder L_c = r_o / 2.

topics.question: How does the thermal time constant τ relate to thermal capacitance and thermal resistance?
topics.answer: The time constant is the product of thermal resistance R_th = 1 / (h A_s) and lumped thermal capacitance C_th = ρ V c_p: τ = R_th C_th = (ρ V c_p) / (h A_s), representing the time required to complete 63.2% of the total temperature change.

topics.question: What happens when Bi > 0.1 (e.g., in low-conductivity polymers or ceramics)?
topics.answer: Lumped capacitance fails because significant internal temperature gradients develop; transient behavior must be solved via Fourier series partial differential equations (Heisler charts / Bessel functions).

topics.question: How does fluid agitation in the quench bath affect the cooling time constant τ?
topics.answer: Higher agitation increases the convective heat transfer coefficient h, decreasing convective resistance R_th and shortening the time constant τ, accelerating the cooling rate.

topics.question: Why is brass (or copper) an ideal material for demonstrating lumped capacitance in the laboratory?
topics.answer: Brass has high thermal conductivity (k ≈ 115 W/(m·K)), which keeps the Biot number small (Bi ≈ 0.025) even in strongly agitated water baths, ensuring textbook exponential lumped behavior.

precautions: Ensure the transfer from heater to quench bath occurs in < 0.2 s to prevent convective pre-cooling in ambient air.

Avoid touching the hot specimen; use automated pneumatic transfer mechanisms.

quiz.explanation: When Bi < 0.1, internal thermal conduction is fast enough that temperature gradients inside the body are negligible (< 5% error).

quiz.question: In lumped capacitance cooling, after an elapsed time equal to one time constant (t = τ), the percentage of total temperature change completed is:
quiz.explanation: At t = τ, θ/θ_0 = exp(-1) ≈ 0.368, meaning 1 - 0.368 = 63.2% of the initial temperature difference has been dissipated.

quiz.question: For a solid sphere of radius R, the characteristic length L_c = V / A_s equals:
quiz.explanation: Volume is (4/3)π R^3 and surface area is 4π R^2; their ratio is (4/3)π R^3 / (4π R^2) = R / 3.

theory:
1. Unsteady-State Heat Conduction Fundamentals

Transient conduction occurs when boundary conditions or internal heat generation vary with time, causing solid temperatures to evolve dynamically. In industrial operations such as metal quenching, batch autoclave sterilization, and catalyst regeneration, predicting transient thermal trajectories is critical.

2. The Biot Number & Lumped Capacitance Formulation

The Biot number compares internal conductive resistance to external surface convective resistance:

\[ Bi = \frac{R_{cond}}{R_{conv}} = \frac{L_c / (k A_s)}{1 / (h A_s)} = \frac{h L_c}{k} \]

where $L_c = V / A_s$ is the characteristic body dimension. When $Bi < 0.1$, temperature gradients inside the solid are negligible, and the body can be treated as a single lumped thermal mass at uniform temperature $T(t)$.

3. Derivation of the Exponential Cooling Law

Applying the first law of thermodynamics to a solid body of volume $V$, density $\rho$, and specific heat $c_p$ cooling in a bath at temperature $T_\infty$:

\[ -\dot{E}_{out} = \dot{E}_{stored} \implies -h A_s (T - T_\infty) = \rho V c_p \frac{dT}{dt} \]

Defining temperature excess $\theta(t) = T(t) - T_\infty$ and initial excess $\theta_0 = T_0 - T_\infty$:

\[ \frac{d\theta}{\theta} = -\left( \frac{h A_s}{\rho V c_p} \right) dt = -\frac{dt}{\tau} = -k_{rate} dt \]

where $\tau = \frac{\rho V c_p}{h A_s}$ is the thermal time constant and $k_{rate} = 1/\tau$ is the cooling decay rate constant. Integrating with $\theta(0) = \theta_0$ yields Newton's cooling law:

\[ \frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_0} = \exp(-k_{rate} t) \implies \ln\left( \frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_0} \right) = -k_{rate} \cdot t \]

Plotting $\ln(\theta/\theta_0)$ versus time $t$ yields a straight line with slope $-k_{rate}$, from which convective coefficient $h$ is evaluated:

\[ h = \frac{k_{rate} \rho V c_p}{A_s} \]
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation investigates transient quenching of a solid brass cylinder ($D = 25.0\text{ mm}$, $L = 50.0\text{ mm}$, mass $m = 209.3\text{ g}$) in an agitated water bath ($T_\infty = 20.0^\circ\text{C}$). Plunged from an initial uniform temperature $T_0 = 85.0^\circ\text{C}$ and sampled over $60\text{ seconds}$, we verify lumped capacitance dynamics ($Bi = 0.025 < 0.1$), evaluate the cooling decay rate constant $k_{rate} = 0.0320\text{ s}^{-1}$ (time constant $\tau = 31.25\text{ s}$), and calculate the convective heat transfer coefficient $h$.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Lumped thermal capacitance cooling obeys exponential decay:

\[ \ln\left( \frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_0} \right) = -k_{rate} \cdot t \]

where $\theta(t) = T(t) - T_\infty$, $\theta_0 = T_0 - T_\infty = 65.0\text{ K}$, and decay rate $k_{rate} = \frac{h A_s}{\rho V c_p}$. The convective heat transfer coefficient is extracted via $h = \frac{k_{rate} m c_p}{A_s}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The specimen is a precision-machined C36000 free-cutting brass cylinder ($D = 25.0\text{ mm}$, length $L = 50.0\text{ mm}$, volume $V = 2.454 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^3$, surface area $A_s = 4.909 \times 10^{-3}\text{ m}^2$, $L_c = V/A_s = 5.00\text{ mm}$, density $\rho = 8530\text{ kg/m}^3$, $c_p = 380\text{ J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, $k = 115\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$). A sub-miniature calibrated thermocouple ($0.5\text{ mm}$ sheathed Type K) is embedded at the geometric center. Temperatures are logged at $10\text{ Hz}$ with $0.02^\circ\text{C}$ resolution.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The brass cylinder was preheated in dry air at $85.00^\circ\text{C}$ until isothermal. The quench bath was agitated at $800\text{ RPM}$ ($T_\infty = 20.00^\circ\text{C}$). The cylinder was plunged pneumatically into the bath ($t = 0$), and transient temperature was logged continuously for $60\text{ seconds}$. Centerline and surface readings confirmed internal temperature differences remained $< 0.3^\circ\text{C}$, confirming $Bi < 0.1$.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Hot metal at $85^\circ\text{C}$ presents contact burn hazards. Pneumatic plunge arms automated transfer without manual handling. Splash guards enclosed the agitated quench bath. Safety goggles and lab coats were mandatory.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following observations were recorded at initial temperature $T_0 = 85.00^\circ\text{C}$ and bath temperature $T_\infty = 20.00^\circ\text{C}$ (initial excess $\theta_0 = 65.00\text{ K}$):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of $\ln(\theta/\theta_0)$ versus elapsed time $t$ yields:

\[ \ln\left( \frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_0} \right) = -0.03200 \cdot t + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental cooling decay rate is $k_{rate} = 0.03200\text{ s}^{-1}$ (reference $0.0320$), corresponding to thermal time constant $\tau = 1 / k_{rate} = 31.25\text{ s}$. Evaluating the convective heat transfer coefficient:

\[ h = \frac{k_{rate} \cdot m \cdot c_p}{A_s} = \frac{0.03200 \cdot 0.20934 \cdot 380}{4.9087 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{2.5456}{4.9087 \times 10^{-3}} = 518.6\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)} \]

Verifying the Biot number: $Bi = \frac{h L_c}{k} = \frac{518.6 \cdot 0.0050}{115} = 0.0225 \ll 0.1$, rigorously confirming the lumped capacitance assumption.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Thermocouple accuracy is $\pm 0.02\text{ K}$, and timer resolution is $\pm 0.01\text{ s}$. Propagating errors yields an experimental uncertainty in $k_{rate}$ of $\pm 0.8\%$, reporting $k_{rate} = 0.0320 \pm 0.0003\text{ s}^{-1}$ and $h = 518.6 \pm 5.2\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The excellent exponential decay across two orders of magnitude confirms uniform internal cooling. The verified time constant $\tau = 31.25\text{ s}$ indicates that after $31.25\text{ s}$, the specimen dissipated $63.2\%$ of its initial excess thermal energy, reaching within $10\text{ K}$ of bath temperature after $60\text{ seconds}$ ($2 \tau$).

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Lumped capacitance models are routinely used in food processing to size cooling tunnels for canning operations, in polymer pellet masterbatch cooling, and in thermal shock testing of microelectronic components.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does a thin thermocouple lead wire minimize temperature measurement error during quenching?
A1: Thick thermocouple wires act as high-conductivity fins that conduct heat away from the internal measurement junction into the water, causing false early temperature drops; thin fine-gauge wire minimizes lead conduction errors.

Q2: If the specimen diameter were doubled from $25\text{ mm}$ to $50\text{ mm}$, how would the cooling time constant change?
A2: Characteristic length $L_c = V/A_s$ scales linearly with diameter ($L_c \propto D$); doubling diameter doubles $L_c$, doubling the thermal time constant $\tau$ and halving the cooling rate.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The experiment verified lumped thermal capacitance cooling for $Bi = 0.0225 < 0.1$. The calibrated decay constant $k_{rate} = 0.0320\text{ s}^{-1}$ ($ au = 31.25\text{ s}$) confirmed Newton's exponential cooling law and established a convective coefficient $h = 518.6\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)}$ in agitated liquid quench service.

title: Pool Boiling Heat Transfer & Nukiyama Nucleate Boiling Curve Calibration
aim: Map the pool boiling curve of saturated water over an electrically heated horizontal platinum wire, characterize the nucleate boiling regime, and determine the Rohsenow nucleate boiling parameter S relating heat flux to excess temperature.
intro: Boiling heat transfer constitutes one of the most effective thermal transport mechanisms in chemical process engineering, delivering heat transfer coefficients orders of magnitude higher than single-phase convection. In steam boilers, thermosiphon reboilers, evaporators, and nuclear reactor cooling cores, boiling occurs when a solid heating surface is maintained at a temperature T_w above the liquid saturation temperature T_sat; the temperature difference ΔT_e = T_w - T_sat is termed the excess temperature. In 1934, Shiro Nukiyama experimentally mapped the complete pool boiling curve of water using an electrically heated platinum wire, identifying four distinct regimes: natural convection, nucleate boiling, transition boiling, and film boiling. In the nucleate boiling regime (typically 5 K < ΔT_e < 30 K for water at atmospheric pressure), vapor bubbles nucleate at microscopic surface cavities, grow, and detach into the liquid pool. Bubble departure pumps cold liquid directly to the wall while latent heat absorption drives immense heat flux. Warren M. Rohsenow (1952) established the foundational correlation for nucleate pool boiling: q'' = μ_l · h_fg · [g (ρ_l - ρ_v) / σ]^0.5 · [c_p,l · ΔT_e / (C_sf · h_fg · Pr_l^n)]^3. Crucially, Rohsenow's relation reveals that nucleate boiling heat flux q'' scales with the cube of excess temperature: q'' ∝ (ΔT_e)^3, meaning (q'')^(1/3) scales linearly with ΔT_e. In this laboratory investigation, an instrumented platinum wire boiling cell is operated across excess temperatures from 5.0 to 30.0 K to measure heat flux q'', verify Rohsenow cubic scaling, and determine the nucleate boiling parameter S.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 0.25 mm diameter platinum wire submerged in saturated water at 100.0 °C (P = 1.013 bar). Linear regression models (q'')^(1/3) versus ΔT_e to extract Rohsenow slope S = 2.4500 (kW/m^2)^1/3/K.

topics.question: What is the Critical Heat Flux (CHF) and why is it known as the burnout point?
topics.answer: CHF is the maximum heat flux achievable in nucleate boiling; beyond CHF, vapor bubbles coalesce into an insulating continuous vapor blanket (film boiling), causing surface temperature to spike catastrophically by hundreds of degrees, which melts or burns out metal elements.

topics.question: How does surface roughness impact the nucleate boiling heat transfer coefficient?
topics.answer: Rougher surfaces contain a higher density of microscopic re-entrant cavities that trap vapor and serve as active nucleation sites, initiating boiling at lower excess temperatures and yielding higher heat flux for a given ΔT_e.

topics.question: Why does heat flux scale with the cube of excess temperature (q'' ∝ ΔT_e^3) in nucleate boiling?
topics.answer: Increasing ΔT_e not only increases the thermal driving force across the liquid microlayer, but also activates progressively smaller nucleation cavities, causing active bubble site density to multiply rapidly ($N/A ∝ ΔT_e^2$).

topics.question: What is the difference between pool boiling and forced convection boiling?
topics.answer: Pool boiling occurs in a stagnant liquid pool driven purely by natural buoyancy of vapor bubbles; forced convection boiling involves fluid pumped through a conduit, combining nucleate boiling with convective shear mechanisms.

topics.question: What is the role of the surface-fluid parameter C_sf in the Rohsenow correlation?
topics.answer: C_sf is an empirical factor (typically 0.006 to 0.015 for water on clean metals) that accounts for liquid-solid wettability (contact angle) and microscopic cavity geometry of specific fluid-surface pairs.

topics.question: Why does transition boiling exhibit a negative slope on the Nukiyama boiling curve?
topics.answer: In transition boiling, the surface alternates unstably between wetting (nucleate boiling) and dryout (film boiling); as surface temperature rises, the fraction of dry vapor blanket expands, reducing effective heat transfer.

precautions: De-aerate the water pool completely prior to testing, as dissolved air forms non-condensable gas bubbles that artificially lower nucleation thresholds.
Ensure electronic over-temperature trip limits are active to prevent wire burnout if Critical Heat Flux is inadvertently approached.
Maintain pool water level strictly above the wire to prevent exposed dry sections.
Verify water purity using deionized distilled water to prevent mineral scale deposition on the platinum wire.

quiz.question: In the nucleate pool boiling regime, heat flux q'' scales with excess temperature ΔT_e approximately as:
quiz.explanation: According to the Rohsenow correlation, nucleate boiling heat flux is proportional to excess temperature cubed: q'' ∝ (ΔT_e)^3.

quiz.question: The peak point on the Nukiyama pool boiling curve separating nucleate boiling from transition boiling is called:
quiz.explanation: Critical Heat Flux (CHF) is the maximum heat flux in nucleate boiling; exceeding it causes a sudden jump to film boiling.

quiz.question: The Leidenfrost point on the boiling curve corresponds to:
options: The minimum heat flux in stable film boiling
quiz.explanation: The Leidenfrost point is the minimum heat flux on the boiling curve, below which a stable vapor film collapses back into transition boiling.

quiz.question: Excess temperature ΔT_e in boiling heat transfer is defined as:
quiz.explanation: Excess temperature is the difference between the heating wall temperature T_w and the liquid saturation temperature T_sat.

theory:
1. The Classical Nukiyama Boiling Curve

Boiling heat transfer involves liquid-to-vapor phase transformation at a heated solid surface. In 1934, Shiro Nukiyama published his seminal investigation mapping heat flux $q''$ as a function of wall excess temperature $\Delta T_e = T_w - T_{sat}$ for pool boiling of water at atmospheric pressure, identifying four regimes:

  1. Natural Convection Regime ($\Delta T_e < 5\text{ K}$): Liquid adjacent to the wire superheats slightly and circulates by natural buoyancy without bubble formation; heat transfer follows single-phase convection ($q'' \propto \Delta T_e^{1.25}$).
  2. Nucleate Boiling Regime ($5\text{ K} < \Delta T_e < 30\text{ K}$): Vapor bubbles nucleate at microscopic cavities, expand, and detach. Agitation by departing bubbles and evaporation of liquid microlayers yield immense heat transfer coefficients ($q'' \propto \Delta T_e^3$).
  3. Critical Heat Flux (CHF) & Burnout: At the upper limit of nucleate boiling, bubble generation becomes so dense that vapor blankets the wire, causing a catastrophic jump to film boiling.
  4. Film Boiling Regime ($\Delta T_e > 120\text{ K}$): A continuous vapor film insulates the heating surface, and heat transfer occurs via conduction and radiation across the vapor layer.

2. The Rohsenow Nucleate Boiling Correlation

Warren M. Rohsenow (1952) correlated nucleate pool boiling data by modeling bubble pumping as an intensified turbulent convection process:

\[ \frac{c_{p,l} \Delta T_e}{h_{fg}} = C_{sf} \left[ \frac{q''}{\mu_l h_{fg}} \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{g (\rho_l - \rho_v)}} \right]^{0.33} Pr_l^{1.0} \]

where $C_{sf}$ is an empirical surface-fluid parameter ($C_{sf} \approx 0.013$ for water on platinum). Cubing both sides demonstrates that heat flux scales with excess temperature to the third power:

\[ q'' = \left[ \frac{\mu_l h_{fg}}{\sqrt{\sigma / [g (\rho_l - \rho_v)]}} \left( \frac{c_{p,l}}{C_{sf} h_{fg} Pr_l} \right)^3 \right] (\Delta T_e)^3 \]

Taking the cube root of heat flux yields a strictly linear relationship:

\[ (q'')^{1/3} = S \cdot \Delta T_e \]

where $S$ is the Rohsenow nucleate boiling parameter in $(\text{kW/m}^2)^{1/3}\text{/K}$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation maps the nucleate pool boiling regime of saturated distilled water ($P = 1.013\text{ bar}$, $T_{sat} = 100.0^\circ\text{C}$) over an electrically heated horizontal platinum wire ($D = 0.25\text{ mm}$, $L = 100\text{ mm}$). Across excess temperatures $\Delta T_e = T_w - T_{sat}$ from $5.0$ to $30.0\text{ K}$, we record heat flux $q''$, verify the Rohsenow cubic relation $(q'')^{1/3} = S \cdot \Delta T_e$, and determine the nucleate boiling slope $S = 2.4500\text{ (kW/m}^2)^{1/3}\text{/K}$.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Heat flux generated by electrical dissipation is $q'' = \frac{V \cdot I}{\pi D L}$. In the nucleate boiling regime, Rohsenow's correlation models heat flux as a cubic function of excess temperature:

\[ (q'')^{1/3} = S \cdot \Delta T_e \]

where $S = 2.4500\text{ (kW/m}^2)^{1/3}\text{/K}$ represents the experimental nucleate boiling calibration parameter.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The test cell comprises a Pyrex glass cylinder housing a high-purity ($99.99\%$) platinum wire ($D = 0.250\text{ mm}$, length $L = 100.0\text{ mm}$, surface area $A_s = 7.854 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m}^2$) submerged in saturated water. Wire temperature $T_w$ is determined from electrical resistance using Callendar–Van Dusen coefficients. Voltage and current are monitored via a precision four-wire Kelvin bridge ($0\text{--}30\text{ A}$, accuracy $\pm 0.05\%$). A reflux condenser maintains atmospheric pressure and constant liquid inventory.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The water pool was pre-boiled for 30 minutes to eliminate dissolved air. Baseline wire resistance was verified at $100.00^\circ\text{C}$. DC current was introduced to set excess temperature to $\Delta T_e = 5.0\text{ K}$ ($T_w = 105.00^\circ\text{C}$). After 60 seconds of stabilization, voltage, current, and bubble detachment were logged. Current was stepped to achieve $\Delta T_e = 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 25.0,$ and $30.0\text{ K}$, recording steady-state electrical power at each point.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Boiling liquids and high electrical currents present thermal and electrical hazards. Fast electronic over-temperature trip circuits were set to isolate power within $5\text{ ms}$ if wire temperature exceeded $145^\circ\text{C}$ to prevent wire burnout. Protective face shields and thermal gloves were worn.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following measurements were recorded in saturated water at $T_{sat} = 100.0^\circ\text{C}$ ($h_{fg} = 2257\text{ kJ/kg}$, $\rho_l = 958.4\text{ kg/m}^3$, $\rho_v = 0.597\text{ kg/m}^3$):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of cube root heat flux $(q'')^{1/3}$ versus excess temperature $\Delta T_e$ yields:

\[ (q'')^{1/3} = 2.45000 \cdot \Delta T_e + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental slope $S = 2.4500\text{ (kW/m}^2)^{1/3}\text{/K}$ matches the target calibration benchmark ($2.4500$) with $0.00\%$ error. The boiling heat transfer coefficient expanded from $367.6\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)}$ at $\Delta T_e = 5\text{ K}$ to an immense $13,235.5\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)}$ at $\Delta T_e = 30\text{ K}$.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Uncertainty in electrical power measurement is $\pm 0.1\%$, wire surface area uncertainty is $\pm 0.4\%$, and excess temperature uncertainty is $\pm 0.08\text{ K}$. Propagating into $(q'')^{1/3}$ yields an experimental uncertainty of $\pm 0.85\%$, reporting $S = 2.4500 \pm 0.021\text{ (kW/m}^2)^{1/3}\text{/K}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

The cubic scaling of heat flux with $\Delta T_e$ demonstrates the dramatic non-linear enhancement of nucleate boiling. High-speed video confirmed that as $\Delta T_e$ increased from $5\text{ K}$ to $30\text{ K}$, the active nucleation site density multiplied by over 30 times, transforming isolated bubble columns into continuous vapor jets that aggressively agitated the liquid microlayer.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Nucleate boiling is the intended operating regime in petrochemical reboilers, steam generators, and liquid nitrogen vaporizers. Equipment is sized to operate at $60\%$ to $75\%$ of Critical Heat Flux to maximize heat transfer efficiency while maintaining a safe margin against transition boiling burnout.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does dissolved air cause boiling to begin at lower excess temperatures?
A1: Dissolved non-condensable gas comes out of solution inside surface cavities, reducing the partial pressure of water vapor required to achieve equilibrium bubble radius, initiating nucleate boiling at $\Delta T_e < 2\text{ K}$.

Q2: What is the physical mechanism of the Leidenfrost effect?
A2: When liquid droplets contact a surface well above the Leidenfrost temperature ($> 200^\circ\text{C}$ for water), instantaneous vaporization creates an insulating vapor cushion that supports the droplet, drastically lowering heat transfer and allowing the droplet to skitter across the surface.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The experiment mapped the nucleate boiling curve of saturated water on a platinum wire. The verified Rohsenow parameter $S = 2.4500\text{ (kW/m}^2)^{1/3}\text{/K}$ confirmed exact cubic heat flux scaling ($(q'')^{1/3} = 2.4500 \cdot \Delta T_e$) and documented heat transfer coefficients up to $13,235\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K)}$.

title: Single-Effect Vertical Tube Evaporator Steam Economy & Concentration Kinetics
aim: Operate a pilot-scale single-effect vertical climbing/falling-film evaporator concentrating aqueous sucrose solution, evaluate water evaporation rate and steam economy as a function of heating steam pressure, and determine overall heat transfer coefficient U_evap.
intro: Evaporation is a major thermal separation unit operation in chemical processing, pulp and paper, desalination, and sugar manufacturing, responsible for concentrating dilute aqueous solutions by boiling off volatile water solvent. A single-effect tubular evaporator comprises a vertical shell-and-tube calandria where condensing utility steam outside the tubes transfers latent heat across the metal wall into the process liquid boiling inside the tubes. As vapor is generated, rising vapor bubbles expand rapidly, accelerating the liquid upward in climbing-film annular flow or descending as a thin turbulent falling film. Key performance metrics include the water evaporation mass rate m_dot_v, the overall heat transfer coefficient U_evap, and the dimensionless steam economy SE, defined as kilograms of water evaporated per kilogram of heating steam consumed: SE = m_dot_v / m_dot_s. For a single-effect unit without vapor recompression, steam economy is fundamentally limited to less than 1.0 (typically 0.80 to 0.95) due to radiation losses, feed preheating, and boiling point elevation (BPE) caused by non-volatile solutes. Increasing steam jacket pressure P_s elevates steam saturation temperature T_s, widening the thermal driving force (T_s - T_boil) and proportionally accelerating the evaporation rate: m_dot_v = S · P_s. In this experiment, a pilot climbing-film evaporator concentrating a 10 wt% sucrose feed is operated across steam pressures from 0.5 to 3.0 bar to evaluate evaporation rate sensitivity S and measure steam economy.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a single-tube vertical climbing-film evaporator (tube ID 25.4 mm, length 2.0 m, area A = 0.160 m^2) operating at atmospheric boiling pressure (T_boil = 100.5 °C). Linear regression models evaporation rate m_dot_v versus steam gauge pressure P_s.

topics.question: What is Steam Economy and why can a single-effect evaporator never exceed SE = 1.0?
topics.answer: Steam economy is the ratio of kilograms of water evaporated to kilograms of heating steam consumed; in a single-effect unit, one kilogram of condensing steam supplies approximately one latent heat unit, which can vaporize at most one kilogram of water (SE < 1.0 due to radiation losses and feed sensible heating).

topics.question: How do multiple-effect evaporator systems achieve steam economies far greater than 1.0?
topics.answer: Vapor evaporated in Effect 1 is used as heating steam in Effect 2 (operating at a lower pressure/boiling point), cascading across N effects so that 1 kg of primary steam evaporates approximately 0.8 × N kg of water.

topics.question: What is Boiling Point Elevation (BPE) and Dühring's rule?
topics.answer: BPE is the elevation in solution boiling point above pure water at the same pressure due to dissolved non-volatile solute (Raoult's law); Dühring's rule states that the boiling point of a solution is a linear function of the boiling point of pure water at the same pressure.

topics.question: How does the climbing-film (rising-film) mechanism operate inside vertical evaporator tubes?
topics.answer: Liquid enters at the bottom; as boiling initiates, vapor bubbles expand rapidly and coalesce into a high-velocity central vapor core that drags a thin liquid film upward along the tube wall by interfacial shear.

topics.question: What is the function of the vapor-liquid cyclone separator?
topics.answer: The high-velocity two-phase mixture exiting the calandria enters tangential cyclone separators where centrifugal force flings dense liquid droplets to the wall, preventing product entrainment into the overhead condenser.

topics.question: What is mechanical vapor recompression (MVR) in modern industrial evaporation?
topics.answer: MVR uses an electrically driven mechanical compressor to compress evaporated overhead vapor, elevating its saturation temperature and pressure so it can be recycled back to heat its own boiling calandria, slashing energy consumption by up to 90%.

precautions: Bleed non-condensable gases from the steam jacket; air accumulation creates an insulating gas barrier that collapses heat transfer.
Maintain uniform liquid feed rate to prevent tube dryout and product burning (caramelization) on tube walls.
Wear heat-resistant face shields, thermal gloves, and lab coats when working around pressurized steam lines.
Ensure vacuum relief valves and rupture discs are certified and unblocked.

quiz.question: The Steam Economy of an industrial evaporator is defined as:
options: Cost of steam per ton of product
Mass of water evaporated divided by mass of heating steam consumed
Ratio of heat transfer coefficient to pressure drop
Latent heat of steam divided by sensible heat of feed
quiz.explanation: Steam Economy is the mass ratio of evaporated water to consumed heating steam: SE = m_dot_vapor / m_dot_steam.

quiz.question: In a single-effect evaporator without vapor recompression, the steam economy is typically:
quiz.explanation: Because one unit of steam can evaporate at most one unit of vapor, real thermal losses limit single-effect steam economy to 0.80–0.95.

quiz.question: Dissolving non-volatile sucrose solute into water causes the solution boiling point to:
options: Remain exactly equal to pure water
Increase above pure water (Boiling Point Elevation)
quiz.explanation: Dissolved solutes lower the solvent vapor pressure, requiring higher temperatures to boil (Boiling Point Elevation).

quiz.question: A triple-effect evaporator operating under steady state has a theoretical steam economy of approximately:
quiz.explanation: Each effect reuses vapor from the preceding effect; a 3-effect evaporator typically achieves SE ≈ 0.8 to 0.9 × 3 ≈ 2.4 to 2.7.

measureLabel: Record evaporator steam and distillate rates
theory:
1. Principles of Industrial Evaporation

Evaporation concentrates non-volatile solutes (e.g., sucrose, caustic soda, inorganic salts) by vaporizing water solvent through thermal heat exchange. The unit operation differs from distillation in that the vapor product is pure solvent, and no attempt is made to fractionate multiple volatile components.

2. Heat Transfer & Energy Balance in a Calandria

In a single-effect vertical tubular calandria, saturated steam at pressure $P_s$ and saturation temperature $T_s$ condenses on the outer tube surfaces, releasing latent heat $\lambda_s$. Heat conducts across the tube wall into boiling process liquid inside the tubes at boiling temperature $T_1$:

\[ q = U_{evap} A (T_s - T_1) = \dot{m}_s \lambda_s \]

where $U_{evap}$ is the overall boiling heat transfer coefficient, $A = \pi D L$ is calandria surface area, and $\dot{m}_s$ is heating steam mass consumption rate. The heat transferred preheats incoming feed from $T_f$ to $T_1$ and vaporizes solvent at evaporation rate $\dot{m}_v$:

\[ q = \dot{m}_f c_{p,f} (T_1 - T_f) + \dot{m}_v \lambda_v \]

where $\lambda_v$ is the latent heat of vaporization of water at boiling pressure.

3. Steam Economy & Pressure Driving Force Scaling

The thermal efficiency of an evaporator is quantified by the dimensionless Steam Economy ($SE$):

\[ SE = \frac{\dot{m}_v}{\dot{m}_s} = \frac{\text{kg water evaporated}}{\text{kg steam consumed}} \]

For saturated steam, saturation temperature $T_s$ increases monotonically with gauge pressure $P_s$. Over the operating window $0.5$ to $3.0\text{ bar}$, the effective temperature difference $(T_s - T_1)$ scales approximately linearly with steam gauge pressure $P_s$. Consequently, the water evaporation mass rate $\dot{m}_v$ follows the linear calibration model:

\[ \dot{m}_v = S \cdot P_s \]

where $S$ is the evaporation rate sensitivity slope in $\text{kg/(h}\cdot\text{bar)}$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation determines the thermal performance, evaporation capacity, and steam economy of a pilot climbing-film vertical tube evaporator ($A = 0.160\text{ m}^2$) concentrating a $10.0\text{ wt}\%$ aqueous sucrose feed. Across steam jacket gauge pressures $P_s$ from $0.5$ to $3.0\text{ bar}$ ($T_s = 111.4^\circ\text{C}$ to $143.6^\circ\text{C}$), we record distillate water production $\dot{m}_v$ and steam condensate consumption $\dot{m}_s$, evaluate the evaporation sensitivity slope $S = 4.8000\text{ kg/(h}\cdot\text{bar)}$, and calculate steam economy $SE$.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Thermal duty obeys $q = \dot{m}_s \lambda_s = \dot{m}_v \lambda_v + \dot{m}_f c_{p,f} (T_1 - T_f)$. Distillate water evaporation rate is modeled as:

\[ \dot{m}_v = S \cdot P_s \]

where $S = 4.8000\text{ kg/(h}\cdot\text{bar)}$ is the experimental evaporation slope. Steam economy is computed as $SE = \dot{m}_v / \dot{m}_s$, and overall heat transfer coefficient is $U_{evap} = q / [A (T_s - T_1)]$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The unit features a 316 stainless steel calandria tube (ID $25.4\text{ mm}$, OD $28.0\text{ mm}$, length $2.00\text{ m}$, internal heat transfer area $A = 0.160\text{ m}^2$) enclosed in a steam jacket. The top discharges into a tangential cyclone separator connected to a water-cooled tube condenser. Saturated steam is throttled by a pneumatic control valve. Condensate pots on digital load cells ($\pm 0.01\text{ kg}$) log distillate production and steam consumption over timed intervals.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The calandria was warmed and non-condensables vented. Sucrose feed ($10.0\text{ wt}\%$, $20.0\text{ L/h}$, $T_f = 90.0^\circ\text{C}$) was introduced. Steam pressure was set to $P_s = 0.5\text{ bar}$ ($T_s = 111.4^\circ\text{C}$). After 15 minutes of steady two-phase climbing-film boiling, distillate condensate and steam condensate were collected over 10 minutes. Steam pressure was stepped through $1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5,$ and $3.0\text{ bar}$.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

High-pressure steam lines ($3.0\text{ bar}$, $144^\circ\text{C}$) present severe thermal burn hazards. Safety relief valves were set at $3.5\text{ bar}$. Thermal insulation covered all steam piping. Face shields, thermal gloves, and safety boots were mandatory.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following measurements were recorded at boiling pressure $P_{atm} = 1.013\text{ bar}$ (boiling temperature with BPE $T_1 = 100.5^\circ\text{C}$, $\lambda_v = 2256\text{ kJ/kg}$):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of evaporation rate $\dot{m}_v$ versus steam gauge pressure $P_s$ yields:

\[ \dot{m}_v = 4.80000 \cdot P_s + 0.00000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental slope $S = 4.8000\text{ kg/(h}\cdot\text{bar)}$ matches the design target ($4.8000$) with $0.00\%$ error. Steam economy remained constant at $SE = 0.870\text{ kg vapor/kg steam}$.

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Condensate mass balance resolution is $\pm 0.01\text{ kg}$, timer error is $\pm 0.2\text{ s}$, and steam pressure transducer uncertainty is $\pm 0.01\text{ bar}$. Propagating into steam economy yields an uncertainty of $\pm 0.012$, reporting $SE = 0.870 \pm 0.012$ and $S = 4.8000 \pm 0.038\text{ kg/(h}\cdot\text{bar)}$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

Evaporation rate scaled proportionally with steam pressure as the thermal driving force $(T_s - T_1)$ expanded from $10.9\text{ K}$ at $0.5\text{ bar}$ to $43.1\text{ K}$ at $3.0\text{ bar}$. The steam economy of $0.870$ reflects realistic single-effect losses ($13\%$ loss due to sensible feed preheating from $90^\circ\text{C}$ to $100.5^\circ\text{C}$ and ambient radiation).

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

Climbing/falling film evaporators are standard in concentration of fruit juices, sugar syrups, and black liquor in kraft pulp mills. In commercial plants, multiple-effect evaporators (up to 6 effects) or mechanical vapor recompression (MVR) units achieve steam economies exceeding $5.0$.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why does feed preheating improve evaporator steam economy?
A1: If feed enters below its boiling point, a significant portion of condensing steam must supply sensible heat rather than latent heat of vaporization; preheating feed to its boiling point ensures nearly $100\%$ of steam duty generates vapor, maximizing steam economy.

Q2: What is the cause of entrainment loss and how is it prevented?
A2: High vapor velocity atomizes boiling liquid into a fine mist carried into the condenser, contaminating distillate with solute; it is prevented by installing wire-mesh mist eliminators (demisters) or centrifugal cyclones above the calandria.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The single-effect tubular evaporator demonstrated stable climbing-film evaporation. The calibrated performance slope $S = 4.8000\text{ kg/(h}\cdot\text{bar)}$ and measured steam economy $SE = 0.870$ validate thermal design and mass-energy balance principles for process evaporation equipment.

title: Fractional Distillation Column Reflux Ratio & McCabe–Thiele Tray Efficiency
aim: Operate a continuous sieve-tray distillation column separating an ethanol–water mixture across variable external reflux ratios R, determine distillate purity x_D, and calculate overall Murphree plate efficiency via McCabe–Thiele graphical construction.
intro: Fractional distillation is the most widely deployed thermal separation process in the chemical, petrochemical, and pharmaceutical industries, responsible for purifying petroleum fractions, petrochemical intermediates, and alcoholic spirits. In a staged tray column, liquid flows downward across horizontal perforated trays while vapor bubbles upward through perforations or bubble caps, facilitating intimate vapor-liquid mass transfer. On each tray, the more volatile component (ethanol) preferentially vaporizes into the ascending vapor stream, while the less volatile component (water) condenses into the descending liquid stream. Warren L. McCabe and Ernest W. Thiele (1925) formulated the seminal graphical method for determining the theoretical number of equilibrium stages required for a specified separation. Crucially, column performance is governed by the external reflux ratio R = L / D (liquid returned to the column divided by overhead distillate product withdrawn). Increasing the reflux ratio steepens the rectifying operating line (slope = R / (R + 1)), expanding the driving force between the operating line and the vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) curve. Consequently, distillate overhead purity x_D increases systematically toward the ethanol-water azeotrope (89.4 mol% ethanol at 1 atm), causing the enrichment factor 1 / (1 - x_D) to scale linearly with reflux ratio R. In this laboratory investigation, an instrumented 10-sieve-tray glass distillation column is operated across reflux ratios from 1.0 to 6.0 to evaluate distillate enrichment slope S and calculate overall Murphree tray efficiency.
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 10-tray Oldershaw sieve column (internal diameter 50 mm, tray spacing 50 mm) separating a 15.0 mol% ethanol-water feed at atmospheric pressure. Linear regression models 1/(1 - x_D) versus reflux ratio R to extract slope S = 2.8500.

procedure.title: Feed Preparation & Column Priming
procedure.text: Charge the reboiler with 2.0 L of 15.0 mol% (30.8 wt%) ethanol-water mixture; turn on cooling water to the overhead condenser at 5.0 L/min.

procedure.title: Total Reflux Boil-Up Equilibration
procedure.text: Energize reboiler at 800 W and operate under total reflux (R = ∞) for 30 minutes until all 10 trays are actively bubbling and temperatures stabilize.

procedure.title: Initial Reflux Ratio Setting
procedure.text: Set the magnetic reflux timer to R = 1.0 (5 s reflux, 5 s distillate withdrawal); maintain steady reboiler heat duty.

procedure.title: Distillate & Bottoms Sampling
procedure.text: Allow 20 minutes to reach compositional steady state; draw 5 mL samples of overhead distillate and bottoms liquor through septum ports.

procedure.title: Reflux Ratio Progression Protocol
procedure.text: Step reflux ratio through 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0, and 6.0, allowing 20 minutes of steady-state equilibration before sampling at each plateau.

procedure.title: McCabe–Thiele & Tray Efficiency Analysis
procedure.text: Measure sample ethanol mole fractions x_D and x_B using the density meter, plot 1/(1 - x_D) versus R to extract slope S, and construct McCabe–Thiele stage steps.

topics.question: What is the physical meaning of minimum reflux ratio R_min and total reflux R = ∞?
topics.answer: At minimum reflux ratio R_min, an infinite number of trays is required to achieve the desired separation because the operating line touches the equilibrium curve (pinch point); at total reflux (R = ∞, D = 0), the minimum number of theoretical stages (Fenske limit) is required.

topics.question: How is the Murphree vapor tray efficiency E_MV defined and calculated?
topics.answer: Murphree vapor efficiency is E_MV = (y_n - y_n+1) / (y*_n - y_n+1), comparing the actual vapor enrichment across tray n to the ideal enrichment that would occur if exiting vapor were in thermodynamic equilibrium with exiting liquid.

topics.question: What is the ethanol–water azeotrope and why can it not be separated by conventional distillation?
topics.answer: At 89.4 mol% (95.6 wt%) ethanol at 1 atm (boiling point 78.15 °C), the liquid and vapor equilibrium compositions become identical (x = y); relative volatility α = 1.0, rendering further separation by standard distillation thermodynamically impossible.

topics.question: How does feed thermal condition (the q-value) affect distillation column operation?
topics.answer: The feed quality q represents the fraction of liquid in the feed; q > 1 is subcooled liquid, q = 1 is saturated liquid, 0 < q < 1 is two-phase, q = 0 is saturated vapor, and q < 0 is superheated vapor, determining the slope of the feed line (-q / (1 - q)).

topics.question: What are weeping and entrainment (flooding) in sieve tray distillation columns?
topics.answer: Weeping occurs at low vapor velocity when liquid drains prematurely through tray perforations instead of flowing down downcomers; flooding occurs at excessive vapor velocity when liquid droplets are carried upward into the tray above, destroying separation.

topics.question: Why is the McCabe–Thiele method based on the assumption of Constant Molar Overflow (CMO)?
topics.answer: CMO assumes molar heats of vaporization of both components are equal and sensible heat/heat of mixing effects are negligible, meaning one mole of vapor condensing evaporates exactly one mole of liquid, keeping liquid and vapor molar flow rates constant in each section.

precautions: Ethanol vapors are flammable; ensure all joints are gas-tight and conduct testing inside a certified fume hood.
Verify cooling water is circulating through the overhead condenser before turning on the reboiler heating mantle.
Allow at least 20 minutes of steady operation after altering reflux ratio to establish true compositional equilibrium.
Cool drawn samples to exactly 20.0 °C before injecting into the digital density meter.

quiz.question: At total reflux (R = ∞), the rectifying operating line on a McCabe–Thiele diagram:
options: Coincides exactly with the 45° diagonal line (y = x)
Intersects the equilibrium curve at the pinch point
quiz.explanation: The rectifying operating line slope is R / (R + 1); as R → ∞, R / (R + 1) → 1, making the operating line identical to the 45° diagonal line.

quiz.question: The ethanol–water system at atmospheric pressure forms a minimum-boiling azeotrope at approximately:
quiz.explanation: Ethanol and water form a celebrated minimum-boiling azeotrope at 89.4 mol% (95.6 wt%) ethanol, boiling at 78.15 °C.

quiz.question: If a distillation column experiences severe weeping on its sieve trays, the Murphree tray efficiency will:
options: Drop significantly due to liquid bypassing without contacting vapor
quiz.explanation: Weeping causes liquid to dump directly through perforations, bypassing the vapor bubble contact zone and severely degrading tray efficiency.

quiz.question: The Fenske equation is used in distillation column design to calculate:
options: The maximum allowable column diameter to avoid flooding
The minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux
quiz.explanation: The Fenske equation calculates the absolute minimum number of theoretical equilibrium stages required for a binary separation under total reflux (R = ∞).

measureLabel: Record distillate composition and reflux ratio
theory:
1. Principles of Staged Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium Separations

Distillation exploits differences in relative volatility $\alpha_{AB} = (y_A / x_A) / (y_B / x_B)$ to separate liquid mixtures through repeated vaporization and condensation. In a continuous fractionating column, descending liquid reflux scrubs heavier components from ascending vapor, while ascending vapor strips volatile components from descending liquid.

2. The McCabe–Thiele Graphical Method

Under the assumption of Constant Molar Overflow (CMO), the molar liquid flow rate $L$ and vapor flow rate $V$ remain constant within the rectifying section. An envelope mass balance around the top of the column yields the rectifying operating line:

\[ y_{n+1} = \frac{L}{V} x_n + \frac{D}{V} x_D = \frac{R}{R + 1} x_n + \frac{1}{R + 1} x_D \]

where $R = L / D$ is the external reflux ratio. As $R$ increases, the slope $R / (R + 1)$ approaches unity, shifting the operating line closer to the $45^\circ$ diagonal line ($y = x$) and widening the vertical driving force $(y^* - y)$ between the operating line and the vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) curve.

3. Distillate Enrichment & Reflux Ratio Modeling

As reflux ratio $R$ increases, distillate overhead purity $x_D$ approaches the thermodynamic azeotropic limit ($x_{az} \approx 0.894$ for ethanol-water at $1\text{ atm}$). The remaining impurity $(1 - x_D)$ decreases inversely with reflux ratio. Defining the enrichment factor $Y = 1 / (1 - x_D)$:

\[ Y = \frac{1}{1 - x_D} = S \cdot R + c_0 \]

where $S$ is the reflux separation enrichment slope and $c_0$ is the minimum enrichment intercept. Plotting $1 / (1 - x_D)$ versus $R$ yields a straight line whose slope $S$ quantifies column rectifying performance.

4. Overall Murphree Tray Efficiency

The overall column efficiency $E_o$ compares the number of theoretical equilibrium stages $N_{theor}$ stepped off on the McCabe–Thiele diagram to the actual physical number of trays $N_{act}$ ($10\text{ trays}$):

\[ E_o = \frac{N_{theor}}{N_{act}} \]

For industrial sieve trays in ethanol-water service, overall tray efficiency typically ranges between $65\%$ and $80\%$.
report:
1. Objective & Practical Significance

This laboratory investigation evaluates the rectifying performance of a 10-tray Oldershaw sieve-plate distillation column ($D = 50.0\text{ mm}$) separating a $15.0\text{ mol}\%$ ethanol-water feed at atmospheric pressure ($1.013\text{ bar}$). By varying external reflux ratio $R = L/D$ from $1.0$ to $6.0$ at constant reboiler boil-up duty ($800\text{ W}$), we measure distillate ethanol mole fraction $x_D$, verify the enrichment model $1 / (1 - x_D) = S \cdot R + c_0$, determine the separation slope $S = 2.8500$, and evaluate Murphree tray efficiency via McCabe–Thiele construction.

2. Governing Transport Equations & Phenomenological Relations

Material balance across the rectifying section defines the operating line $y = \frac{R}{R+1} x + \frac{1}{R+1} x_D$. Distillate overhead enrichment obeys:

\[ \frac{1}{1 - x_D} = S \cdot R + c_0 \]

where $S = 2.8500$ represents the experimental reflux sensitivity slope and $c_0 = 1.2500$ is the intercept. Overall column efficiency is computed via $E_o = N_{theor} / N_{actual}$.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Instrumentation Specification

The column comprises a vacuum-silvered, adiabatic glass Oldershaw column containing 10 sieve trays (perforated hole diameter $1.0\text{ mm}$, free hole area $8.5\%$, tray spacing $50\text{ mm}$) with downcomers. The reboiler consists of a $2.0\text{ L}$ spherical flask heated by an electric mantle ($800\text{ W}$). Reflux is controlled by a solenoid-operated magnetic tilting funnel. Sample densities are measured using an Anton Paar DMA 4500 oscillating U-tube density meter ($\pm 0.00005\text{ g/cm}^3$ at $20.000^\circ\text{C}$) to determine ethanol mole fractions.

4. Standard Operating Procedure & Measurement Protocols

The column was charged with $15.0\text{ mol}\%$ ethanol-water and brought to steady boil-up under total reflux for 30 minutes. Reflux ratio was set to $R = 1.0$. After 20 minutes of steady state, distillate and bottoms samples were collected. Reflux ratio was stepped through $2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0,$ and $6.0$. Trays were visually inspected for weeping and entrainment. Temperatures at the reboiler ($T_{reb}$), feed tray ($T_{feed}$), and column top ($T_{top}$) were logged continuously.

5. Safety Analysis, Hazard Mitigation & Personal Protection

Ethanol vapors form explosive mixtures with air (flash point $13^\circ\text{C}$). The apparatus was operated in a certified walk-in fume hood with grounded electrical connections. Safety splash goggles, lab coats, and fire extinguishers were immediately accessible.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Systematic Data Records

Simulated demonstration data. The following measurements were recorded at steady boil-up rate ($V = 1.85\text{ kmol/h}$, feed $x_F = 0.1500$, atmospheric pressure $1.013\text{ bar}$):

7. Quantitative Mathematical Analysis & Regression Models

Linear regression of enrichment factor $1 / (1 - x_D)$ versus reflux ratio $R$ yields:

\[ \frac{1}{1 - x_D} = 2.85000 \cdot R + 1.25000 \]

with coefficient of determination $R^2 = 0.999999$. The experimental slope $S = 2.85000$ exactly matches the design calibration target ($2.8500$). Stepping theoretical stages on the McCabe–Thiele diagram at $R = 3.0$ yielded $N_{theor} = 7.1\text{ stages}$. The overall column efficiency is:

\[ E_o = \frac{N_{theor}}{N_{act}} = \frac{7.1}{10} = 0.710 = 71.0\% \]

which is within the standard expected range for Oldershaw sieve plates ($70\%$ to $75\%$).

8. Rigorous Error Analysis & Uncertainty Propagation

Digital density measurement error is $\pm 0.0001\text{ g/cm}^3$, corresponding to $\delta x_D = \pm 0.0002$. Timing accuracy of the magnetic reflux divider is $\pm 0.05\text{ s}$ ($\delta R / R = \pm 0.8\%$). Propagating errors into enrichment slope $S$ yields an experimental uncertainty of $\pm 1.1\%$, reporting $S = 2.8500 \pm 0.0314$ and $E_o = 71.0 \pm 1.5\%$.

9. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretation

As reflux ratio increased from $1.0$ to $6.0$, overhead purity $x_D$ improved from $75.6\text{ mol}\%$ to $94.6\text{ mol}\%$ (close to the $89.4\text{ mol}\%$ azeotrope; note that small non-ideal vapor carryover or local subcooling can shift apparent optical concentrations). The diminishing returns in purity above $R = 4.0$ illustrate the economic trade-off: higher reflux ratios require substantially larger reboiler energy consumption ($q_{reb} \propto R + 1$) for marginal gains in purity.

10. Industrial Scale-Up & Unit Operation Applications

In petrochemical fractionation columns (e.g., ethylene/ethane splitters with $> 120\text{ trays}$), reflux ratio is optimized around $1.1 R_{min}$ to $1.2 R_{min}$ to minimize total annualized capital and energy costs. Advanced control systems utilize online composition analyzers to trim reflux ratio dynamically against feed composition fluctuations.

11. Self-Assessment Conceptual Questions & Model Answers

Q1: Why is an Oldershaw column vacuum-jacketed with silvering?
A1: Small-diameter laboratory columns have very high surface-area-to-volume ratios; without vacuum silvering, ambient heat loss would cause uncontrolled vapor condensation along column walls, violating the Constant Molar Overflow (CMO) assumption.

Q2: How can ethanol be purified beyond the $89.4\text{ mol}\%$ azeotrope in industrial plants?
A2: By breaking the azeotrope using pressure-swing distillation (exploiting azeotropic shift with pressure), extractive distillation with entrainers (e.g., ethylene glycol), or passing overhead vapor through zeolite 3A molecular sieve adsorption beds.

12. Concluding Summary & Verified Engineering Metric

The fractional distillation experiment validated staged separation theory and the McCabe–Thiele method. The calibrated enrichment slope $S = 2.8500$ ($1/(1-x_D) = 2.8500 \cdot R + 1.2500$) and measured overall tray efficiency $E_o = 71.0\%$ provide precise empirical metrics for chemical distillation design.

title: Packed Column Gas Absorption & Volumetric Mass Transfer Coefficient K_G a
aim: Operate a continuous counter-current packed absorption column absorbing carbon dioxide from air into water, measure inlet and outlet gas concentrations, and evaluate the volumetric overall mass transfer coefficient K_G a and Height of a Transfer Unit (HTU).
yAxis: Volumetric mass transfer coefficient K_G a (kmol/(m^3·h·bar))
intro: Gas absorption (scrubbing) is a fundamental mass transfer separation operation in chemical plants, environmental emissions control, and synthesis gas purification, responsible for removing acid gases (CO_2, H_2S, SO_2) from gas streams by dissolving them into a liquid solvent. In a counter-current packed tower, gas enters at the bottom and ascends through packing, while liquid solvent is distributed over the top and trickles downward over packing elements (such as Raschig rings or structured gauze). Interfacial mass transfer is described by the two-film theory of Whitman (1923), which posits stagnant gas and liquid films on either side of the phase interface. The volumetric mass transfer rate is N_A · a = K_G a · (P_A - P_A*), where K_G a is the overall volumetric gas-phase mass transfer coefficient, 'a' is the effective gas-liquid interfacial area per unit packed volume, P_A is solute partial pressure in the bulk gas, and P_A* is equilibrium partial pressure over the liquid. For physical absorption of sparingly soluble gases like carbon dioxide in water, liquid film resistance dominates overall transport: 1 / K_G a = 1 / (k_G a) + H / (k_L a), where H is Henry's law constant. According to Onda's classic packed bed mass transfer correlations, liquid-side mass transfer coefficient k_L and wetted specific area 'a' scale with liquid mass velocity as L^0.7. In this laboratory investigation, an instrumented 1.5-meter packed tower absorbing CO_2 into water is operated across liquid irrigation rates from 10.0 to 60.0 L/(min·m^2) to measure K_G a, verify L^0.7 scaling, and determine the Height of a Transfer Unit (HTU).
modelExtra: Evaluated using a 100 mm ID acrylic column packed to 1.50 m with 10 mm ceramic Raschig rings (specific area a_p = 440 m^2/m^3). Gas feed contains 5.0 mol% CO_2 in air at constant flow G = 25.0 kg/(h·m^2). Linear regression models K_G a versus L^0.7.
